chapters.title: Dilemma at Noon
paragraphs: After bathing the dry, withered body of Bhagirathi, dressing her in a clean sari, and completing the rituals of worship and offering as prescribed, adorning her hair with the sacred flowers of prasada, giving her tirtha, touching her feet to receive her blessings, Praneshacharya brought the bowl of rava porridge.
“Let your meal be first,” Bhagirathi said in a faint voice.
“No. Let your gruel be first,” he replied.

For twenty years, this exchange had become a ritual between them. The morning bath, the sandhyavandana, cooking, giving medicine to his wife, then crossing the river to perform puja to the temple’s Maruti—these were the unbroken observances. After the meal, the Brahmins of the agrahara would come one by one to his doorstep—to listen to the recitation of the puranas and tales of virtue that had become dear to him day by day. In the evening, again the bath, sandhyavandana, gruel for his wife, medicine, cooking, supper—then, returning to the veranda, the discourse to the Brahmins gathered there.
Now and then, Bhagirathi would say:
“What happiness have you found by tying yourself to me? Doesn’t the house need a child? Marry again.”
“A man as old as I am, to marry again…” Praneshacharya would laugh.

“You haven’t even crossed forty. Which father would not be glad to give his daughter in marriage to one who has studied Sanskrit in Kashi and returned? The house needs a child. Since you took my hand, have you known happiness…?”
Praneshacharya would smile shyly, and as he tried to rise and sit—
Samskara

He is told: Put your wife to bed, let her sleep. Did not the Lord say, perform your duties without desire for the fruits? It is only to test those on the path of liberation that He grants them birth as Brahmins and entangles them in such worldly affairs. The blessed feeling, as sweet as the taste of panchamrita, is followed by repentance that falls upon his wife, and because she is ill, he feels he has grown even more gentle, and takes pride in his own restraint.

Before sitting down to eat, he lifts a handful of grass onto a plantain leaf and places it before Gauri, who is grazing in the backyard. He strokes the cow’s bristling, sacred body, presses his eyes to it, and as he steps inside, he hears a woman’s voice calling, “Acharya, Acharya!” Listening closely, it seems to be Chandri, Narayanappa’s concubine. If he speaks to her, he will have to bathe again before he can eat. But if a woman is left waiting in the courtyard, is it possible for a morsel to pass one’s throat?
He goes to the veranda. Chandri stands there, her sari drawn tightly over her head, pale and stricken with fear.
“What brings you here, child?”
“He… he…”
Chandri, trembling, leans against the pillar, unable to speak.
“Who? Narayanappa? What has happened?”
“He is gone…”
Chandri covers her face.
“Narayana, Narayana—when?”
“Just now…”
“Narayana—what happened?”
Chandri, sobbing, manages to say:
“After returning from Shimoga, he was struck with fever and took to his bed. Four days of fever—nothing more… There was a swelling near his ribs, like a well rising with pain…”
Samskara
“Narayana.”

Praneshacharya, still in his eating clothes, hurried across the agrahara and rushed into Garudacharya’s house, calling out, “Garuda, Garuda!” as he entered the kitchen. Narayanappa was related to Garudacharya through five generations. Narayanappa’s great-grandfather’s grandmother and Garudacharya’s great-grandfather’s grandmother were sisters. Just as Garudacharya was about to lift a morsel of mixed saaru to his mouth—
“Narayana… Garuda, don’t eat. Narayanappa is gone.”
Wiping the sweat off his face, glistening in the midday heat, Praneshacharya delivered the news.

Garudacharya was stunned. Even though he and Narayanappa had, by oath, severed all ties, he left the morsel on the leaf where it was, washed his hands, and stood up. Turning to his wife, Sitadevi, who stood frozen, clutching her sari tightly, he said, “Let the children eat, it doesn’t matter for them. Until the funeral rites are done, we cannot eat.” And he left with Praneshacharya.

Fearing that someone nearby might eat before hearing the news, Praneshacharya hurried to Udupi Lakshmanacharya’s house, while Garudacharya, still dazed, ran to Lakshmi Devamma’s and then to the house of Durgabhatta of the lower street, spreading the word as he went. Like wildfire, the news spread to the remaining ten houses of the agrahara. Children were gathered inside, doors and windows shut tight. By the grace of the gods, not a single Brahmin had eaten yet.

Though not a single woman or child in the agrahara felt any grief at the news of Narayanappa’s death, an unspoken, unfamiliar fear and anxiety took root in every heart. Udupi Lakshmanacharya, cursing his fate for having such an enemy in life, a thorn in death, and now a corpse that had become a problem, washed his hands. Every man who set out to gather in the Acharya’s verandah heard his wife whisper in his ear: “Pranesh—”
Samskara
“Do not agree to perform his funeral rites unless the Acharya himself decides. What will happen if the Guru declares an excommunication tomorrow?”

In the same manner as when they would crowd together to listen to the Purana—yet today, in an unspoken anxiety—the Brahmins gathered in the verandah, and Praneshacharya, circling the tulsi plant with his rosary, spoke as if posing a question to himself:
“Naranappa’s funeral rites must be performed: that is the first question. He has no children—someone must perform his obsequies: that is the second question.”

Chandri, who stood by the pillar in the courtyard, waited anxiously to hear what the Brahmins would say to this. Unable to contain her curiosity, she came from the backyard door. The women, who stood in the midst of the gathering, watched Praneshacharya, worried about what rash thing their husbands might do.
To everything the Acharya said, Garudacharya, rubbing his thick, black arms in his usual way, replied, “Yes, yes, that’s right, that’s right.”
“No one is to eat until the funeral rites are performed, isn’t it?” said Dasacharya, thin as a cow’s tail, one of the poor Brahmins in the group.

“True...true,” said Lakshmanacharya, rubbing his belly, moving his face forward and back, blinking his eyelids. The only part of him that seemed well-fed was his belly, swollen from chronic fever. His sunken cheeks, jaundiced eyes, bony chest, and stick-like legs made his body unbalanced, so he walked with his back arched—thus was he the subject of the Panchagramas’ jokes in Parijatapura.
Seeing that no one was giving a direct answer, Praneshacharya—
Samskara 5

“And so, the problem before us now is: who should perform his funeral rites, his samskara, and the offering of food? The Dharma Shastra says that if there are no close relatives, any Brahmin may perform them.”
Since he had mentioned ‘relatives,’ the other Brahmins turned to look at Garudacharya and Lakshmanacharya.

Lakshmanacharya closed his eyes, as if to say it was not his responsibility. But Garudacharya, who had experience with court matters, felt it necessary to speak now. He took a pinch of snuff, cleared his throat, and said:

“It is right that we act according to the Dharma Shastra. Among us, the words of our great scholar are as sacred as the Veda itself. If you command, so be it. It is true that there is an ancestral connection between him and me. But as you know, his father and I went to court, quarreled over that garden, and after his father died, even though I brought justice from Dharmasthala, this Narayanappa defied the divine order—what then? After we both swore that from now on, for generations to come, there would be no conversation, marriage, sacred thread ceremony, or meals exchanged between our families—what then?”

Garudacharya’s nasal, court-trained speech faltered for a moment, but another pinch of snuff revived him. Gaining courage, he looked around, caught Chandri’s face, and decided there was no need to hide anything:

“The words you have spoken, even our guru would agree with them. Whether I can perform the samskara or not, let that be set aside. The real question is whether he is a Brahmin at all. What?—A man who lived with a shudra woman...”
The agrahara’s only Smartha, Durgabhatta, watched Chandri with a sidelong glance, curious to see how deep this Madhwa orthodoxy ran, and shot back sharply:
“Chi, chi, chi! Don’t be so hasty, Acharya. A Brahmin does not lose his caste the moment he takes a shudra woman as a concubine. From the north to here—”
Samskara

Our ancestors who came here—ask Praneshacharya if you wish—there is a belief in history that they mingled with Dravidian women. I’m not saying this to make fun... If you look at it that way, the worldly folk who go to Dakshina Kannada district are the Basrur courtesans...”
Madhavacharya’s foot was tapping restlessly, and Garudacharya was irritated at his levity:

“Hold on, Durga Bhatta, restrain yourself a little. The question here is not merely about carnal relations. You need not teach Vedantashiroamani Praneshacharya, who went to Kashi and studied Vedanta, about anuloma and pratiloma. What? He has debated with the greatest scholars of your tradition and mine, won accolades in all the southern seats of learning, received fifteen shawls and silver plates as prizes—what?—my Acharya—what?”
Praneshacharya felt awkward, as the conversation had drifted from the main issue to his own praise.
“Lakshmana, what are you saying? Didn’t Narayanappa marry your wife’s younger sister?”
Lakshmanacharya closed his eyes.

“All of it was with your permission, your consent. What do we know of the subtleties of dharma? Narayanappa—as Garuda says—had relations with a woman of a lower caste...” He let the sentence trail off, its meaning clear. Rubbing his nose with his angavastra, he added, “As you know, the question is whether he ate food she cooked...”
“And whether he drank liquor...” Padmanabhacharya, who lived across from Narayanappa’s house, joined in.
“Let liquor be, it’s said he even ate meat,” Garudacharya turned to Durga Bhatta and said, “Even that should not be an obstacle for you. Your own religious teachers, full of experience...

“Didn’t some even enter other bodies and lose themselves with queens?” Sensing the conversation was turning sharp, Praneshacharya said, “Garuda, be a little quiet.” “He abandoned his wedded wife. If you say let that go…” Lakshmanacharya, closing his eyes, began again: “He took up with all sorts of women. He didn’t perform the samskara for my house’s woman—my sister—who died in madness. Let that go too. He didn’t even perform the shraddha for his own father and mother. I never claimed him as my close kin. He was my wife’s mother’s elder brother’s son. We took him in only because he was of our own kind, not because he was truly ours. Let that go too. But in front of all the Brahmins, he came to the river, and the very saligrama stone that had been worshipped in his house for generations—he threw it into the water and spat on it with a ‘thoo’! Let that go too. But then, as if to show us all, he brought in the Turukas and made them drink liquor and eat forbidden food right in his courtyard! If anyone tried to say a word of sense to him, he would heap abuse and shame on them. As long as he lived, we all had to live in fear of him.”

Listening from inside, Anasuya, his wife, felt happy, thinking her husband was speaking up for her sake. Chandri, sitting pressed against the pillar, caught Anasuya’s eye and was cursed in her heart: May a tiger maul her in the dead of night, may a snake bite her. This harlot, this temptress—if she hadn’t bewitched him, would her own cousin, the son of her mother’s brother, have abandoned his own family’s woman, left her to die of sickness, pawned off the family’s gold to hang it around this shaven woman’s neck…? Seeing the gold chain and bangles on Chandri’s neck and hands, Anasuya could not bear her grief and burst into tears. If her own sister were alive, that gold would have adorned her neck. Now her own blood relation’s corpse had to lie unpurified, without samskara…
Samskara
Why? All this happened because of that wretched harlot, didn’t it? She raged, boiling with anger, wishing to set fire to her face.
Dasacharya, whose life was supposed to be sustained by Brahminical charity, who would walk ten miles without complaint for a meal, now poured out his troubles:

“We kept him in our agrahara—as you all know, the santarpane, the Brahminical offering, that too hasn’t come to us for two years now. If, in our haste, we ourselves were to perform his funeral rites, it would mean nothing for Brahminical merit. That is, now, with his corpse lying in the agrahara, it’s not even possible for us to fast, leaving aside food. In this crisis of dharma, Praneshacharya must discern and declare the subtlety of the law. Who among us could challenge his word in our tradition...?”

Feeling this was not a question for him, Durga Bhatta sat apart, examining the chandri. He had never strayed from the common mind, and this object, brought from Kundapura by Narayanappa’s fancy, had caught his connoisseur’s eye for the first time today. It was a vision straight out of Vatsyayana’s descriptions. Look at that finger, longer than a thumb. Look at those breasts—she would drain a man dry in union. Eyes that should have been restless were now faded with sorrow and fear, suffused with a strange tenderness. In his sleeping chamber, on the edge of the Ravi Varma painting he had hung, the nose, eyes, and lips of Matsyagandhi, who had covered her poverty-sold breasts in shame—he remembered how Narayanappa had thrown away the sacred shaligrama for her, how he had eaten meat and drunk wine for her. It was no wonder. His courage was astonishing. He remembered Jagannatha, who had married a Muslim girl, and how the breasts of the mlechha maiden were praised in the Shringara Shataka. Praneshacharya...

If not for this, if Naranappa had not died, even if they were kings, these Brahmins would have simply recited that shloka and explained it away: kāmāturāṇām—meaning, for people like Naranappa—there is neither fear nor shame.

Seeing the gathering fall silent, Durgabhatta said: “We have said all that needed to be said. What is the use of digging up the faults of the dead? Now let Praneshacharya speak. He is as good as a guru to me as well. Let Garudacharya say whatever he wants in his pride of opinion…”

Praneshacharya, weighing each word, aware that the burden of protecting the Brahminhood of the entire agrahara rested on his shoulders, spoke hesitantly: “Garuda said: there was a vow of association between him and Naranappa. For that, there is a remedy in the Dharmashastra. One must perform a shanti, a ritual of atonement. There must be a gift of a cow. One must visit a holy place. These are matters of expense. I do not have the authority to command you to bear this expense.

Then, the question raised by Lakshmana, Das, and the others: Naranappa, though born in a noble Brahmin lineage, did not conduct himself as a Brahmin should; he brought disrepute to the agrahara. This is a grave question. I do not see a clear answer to it. For even though he abandoned Brahminhood, Brahminhood did not abandon him. He was not excommunicated. According to the shastras, since he did not die as an outcaste, he died as a Brahmin. If we consider it thus, those who are not Brahmins have no right to touch his body. If we allow them to touch it, even then, our Brahminhood is tainted.

Even with all this, seeing and knowing the way he lived, I hesitate to insist that you must perform the samskara for him. What is to be done? What does the Dharmashastra say about this? Are there remedies—shanti and such—for this transgression…?”
Samskara

All the Brahmins were astonished. The women gathered at the chāvadi. None could trust their own eyes; Chandri, removing her gold necklace and bangles, placed them before Praneshacharya, saying it was for the expenses of the samskara, and then went to stand where she had first been.

“There must be at least two thousand rupees’ worth of gold here,” the women calculated. One after another, each woman looked at her husband’s face. All the Brahmins lowered their eyes; fear gripped them. Would Brahminhood be destroyed by the lure of gold? They were bewildered. Yet, in the very next moment, a question flashed in every mind: If not me, will some other Brahmin perform Narayanappa’s funeral rites, and without losing his Brahminhood, adorn his wife’s neck with this gold?

The mutual jealousy and resentment between Lakshmanacharya and Garudacharya now flared up even more fiercely because of this new reason. What if, disgracing himself, one of them snatched the gold that should rightfully be his, and without losing his Brahminhood, donated a poor cow as atonement, and thus secured both this world and the next?
Durga Bhatta thought: Let these Madhvas perform Narayanappa’s samskara if they wish; I’ll go from village to village and proclaim to all what a deed they have committed.
Dasacharya and the other poor Brahmins’ mouths watered and their eyes grew moist. When would Garuda or Lakshmana ever let us perform Narayanappa’s rites?
Only Praneshacharya was troubled: “What is this? In the attempt to do good, this Chandri has thrown everything into disorder.”
Each Brahmin, afraid that someone else might agree before him, began to exaggerate the injustice he had suffered from Narayanappa, as if to outdo the others in competition:
“Garudacharya’s son ran away from home and joined the military—”
Samskara 11
Who else but Narayanappa incited all this? Praneshacharya himself taught him the Vedas, and yet, in the end, it was Narayanappa’s words that prevailed—he insisted on corrupting all our boys...

“Now, look at poor Lakshmanacharya’s son-in-law. They raised a boy from a distant land, nurtured him, gave him their daughter in marriage, and even then, Narayanappa managed to spoil his mind. It’s hard to see his face even once a month these days...”

“And if that weren’t enough, there’s that Ganapati—the fish in the lake has belonged to the deity for generations. There’s a belief that anyone who catches it will die a bloody death, but this Chandala ignored all that, brought the Muslims along, set off explosives, and killed the fish. Now even the Shudras and others go there to catch fish. That wretch destroyed the Brahmins’ authority over the others. And as if that weren’t enough, he ruined our agrahara by infecting the boys of Parijatapura with a craze for drama.”
“They should have excommunicated that Chandala. Don’t you agree?”

“How was that ever possible, Garuda? He threatened that if they excommunicated him, he would become a Muslim. On the very day of Prathama Ekadashi, he brought the Turks into the agrahara and hosted a feast. He said, ‘Try excommunicating me—I’ll become a Turk, tie you all to posts, force beef into your mouths, and destroy your Brahminhood.’ If he had really become a Turk, there would have been no way to drive him out of the agrahara. Tell me, what could anyone do in such a predicament? Even Praneshacharya could do nothing but sit with folded hands, could he?”
Dasacharya, agitated because he could not swallow even a morsel of the mixed rice with tamarind sauce and had to rise, added his final words:
“After his father died, not a single Brahmin’s mouth tasted even a slice of the jackfruit honey from his backyard...”
Samskara

The women, who had been watching the gold with greedy eyes, felt disappointed upon hearing their husbands’ words. Sita, Garudacharya’s wife, wondered what right Lakshmanacharya ever had to boast about her son joining the military, and Anasuya, Lakshmanacharya’s wife, felt angered that Garudacharya dared to mention her son-in-law at all.
What kind of trial is this, Praneshacharya thought to himself, as if in a soliloquy:

“What is the way out now…? Is it possible to sit here, hands tied, with a corpse lying in the agrahara? According to Sanatana Dharma, until the corpse is taken out of the agrahara, there can be no worship of the gods, no bathing, no sandhyavandana, no meals, no rituals at all… Since he is not an outcaste, no one but Brahmins can touch his corpse…”
“The fact that he was not excommunicated has left us in this dilemma…”
Garudacharya, who had long agitated for Narayanappa’s excommunication, now spoke in a wounded tone, “You did not listen to me.”
“If he had become a Muslim, we would have had to abandon this agrahara ourselves. We would have been left without any direction…”
All the Brahmins argued together.
Dasacharya, imagining the hardship of going without food all day, suddenly had a flash of inspiration. Rising with delight, he said:
“I have heard that the Brahmins of Parijatapura were friends with Narayanappa. They even shared meals and rituals, it seems. Their achara is not as strict as ours… Let us go and ask them.”
The people of Parijatapura were Adapankti Brahmins; they were Smartas. In the past, when a widow named Basuramma…
Samskara 13

There was always the fear—what if this news reached the gurus at Sringeri and the entire agrahara was excommunicated? The people of Parijatapura, on the whole, were content; they were not ones to dance in the name of ritual purity and observance. They were tireless in tending their areca gardens—prosperous, wealthy. For this reason, Durgabhatta felt a certain affection for them, and, besides, a secret pride that, after all, they were Smartas like himself. It was true that, in secret, he had sometimes enjoyed their avalakki, uppittu, and coffee. He had not yet gone so far as to eat a full meal there—no, not yet.

Apart from matters of business, there was another attraction for him in Parijatapura: the widows who ate the tender areca nuts under the trees, their hair unbound. When Dasacharya’s gossiping became unbearable, Durgabhatta, angered by his words—“This Madhva’s arrogance—even though he has no means to eat”—rose and said:

“What you have spoken is utterly unjust. Even if you think they are lower-caste Brahmins, don’t they themselves feel they are inferior? If your caste is lost by touching the corpse of someone of your own sect, then wouldn’t theirs be lost even more? Why don’t you take the risk and ask them—perform the proper rites and bring them here. Parijatapura’s Manjayya has enough money to buy all of you, you know that, don’t you…?”
To calm Durgabhatta’s anger, Praneshacharya spoke:

“What you say is just, Bhattaru. It is not Brahminhood to make another do what we ourselves will not. But just as blood relations are strong, so too are bonds of friendship, are they not? If it is true that Narayanappa was their friend, surely you will agree that they have a right to know of his death?”

Durgabhatta replied, “Agreed, Acharya. All the Brahminhood of your sect is now in your hands. Your responsibility is great. Who will oppose what you have decided?” And with that, he fell silent, having spoken the truth.
chapters.summary: Praneshacharya faces a moral dilemma when the outcast Narayanappa dies, forcing the local Brahmins to debate ritual purity before they can eat their midday meals.

chapters.title: Scriptures and Shadows
paragraphs: Samskara

Once again, the question of the gold arose. If the people of Parijatapura agreed to perform the samskara, would it be right or wrong for them to receive the gold? Lakshmanacharya’s wife, Anasuya, could not bear the thought that the ornament, which should have adorned her younger sister’s body, would now fall into the hands of those outcast Brahmins. Unable to restrain herself, she burst out:

“Whose property does she think this gold is, that she’s giving it away as if it were her own? If everything had gone as it should, it would have been around my sister’s neck now,” she sobbed bitterly.
Though her words seemed just to Lakshmanacharya, he, not wishing to compromise his dignity as a husband, rebuked her:
“What business do you women have in men’s affairs? Be quiet.”
Garudacharya, angered, thundered, “Well said! According to the law of Dharmasthala, this gold should rightfully come to me.”

Praneshacharya, weary of the bickering, said, “Let us conduct ourselves with patience. What lies before us is a corpse that must undergo samskara. Leave the matter of the gold to me. First, let us send word to the people of Parijatapura. If they wish to come and perform the samskara themselves, let them do so…” he tried to pacify them, then added, “Now, all of you leave. I will search through the Manusmriti and other shastras—perhaps there is an answer to this dilemma,” and he rose to his feet. Chandri, her head covered with her sari, looked at Praneshacharya with desperate hope.
Chapter Two
In the buttermilk pot, an ant; in the granary, a rat; in the central hall, on the wooden platform, a folded sari, a pile of clothes; in the courtyard, left out to dry…
On the chapati pan, there were papads, sandige, and green chilies from the backyard—these were common to every house in the agrahara.

But refinement meant the various flowering trees cultivated in the backyard; in Bhimacharya’s yard grew the parijata, in Padmanabhacharya’s, jasmine; in Lakshmanacharya’s, the flaming red champak; in Garudacharya’s, ranja; in Dasacharya’s, mandara; in Durgabhatta’s, shankhapushpa and bilva leaves. For the daily worship of the gods, each man would go to his own garden to pluck flowers, exchanging greetings with others as he went. Only in Narayanappa’s house were the flowers left to the mercy of Chandri’s broom, or to wilt in the sleeping room. And as if that were not enough, right in front of his house grew the night queen—raat rani—whose flowers, beloved of serpents and unfit for the deity’s crown, were considered tamasic. Clusters upon clusters of its blossoms would burst open in the darkness, spreading their nocturnal fragrance like a heady intoxication; the entire agrahara would be unsettled, as if caught in a serpent’s spell. Those with sensitive noses would cover their faces with the end of their upper cloth as they passed, complaining of headaches.

The wise would say that Narayanappa had planted the night queen as a serpent-guard, so that thieves would not dare approach his hidden gold. While the other married women, with their thick, oiled plaits, would pin mandara or jasmine in their hair, Chandri, with her dark, snake-like tresses, would tuck in the fallen champak or kedage blossoms, swept from the floor.

When night fell, the kingdom of the night queen reigned over the agrahara; by day, the Brahmins carried on their bodies the gentle, auspicious fragrances of sandalwood, parijata, and other soft flowers. In every backyard, there was a jackfruit or mango tree of its own flavor. According to the proverb, “Share the fruit to eat, give the flower to adorn,” the distribution of fruit and flowers was a daily ritual. Only Lakshmanacharya would secretly divide the fruit from his tree and sell it to the Konkani shopkeepers, keeping the profits to himself. He was a miserly soul; when his wife’s relatives visited, he would watch her hands with the eyes of a hawk.
He waits, always watching—wondering where she might stealthily give something to Taure.

In the months of Chaitra and Vaishakha, every house offers charity in the form of kosumbari and panaka; in Kartika, they invite each other for the festival of lights. Narayanappa alone is exempt from all this. On both sides of the agrahara street, there are ten houses in all. The largest of them belongs to Narayanappa—at one end of the street. On one side, the backyard of a neighbor rises up to the Tunga river, and to reach the water, the pious ancestors had built stone steps.

In Shravan, when the Tunga swells, she rages for three or four days as if she will flood the agrahara, becoming a festival of sound and spectacle for the children’s eyes and ears. Then she recedes, and in the heart of summer, she becomes a shimmering stream, split into three channels. At that time, the Brahmins cultivate colored cucumbers and watermelons in the sandy banks, enough vegetables to last through the rainy season. For twelve months of the year, these colored cucumbers hang from the creepers in the plantain grove. In the monsoon, every dish is made of them—palya, huli, gojju, and even a soup from their seeds. Like the Basuris, the Brahmins long for the tangy mango gojju with their rice.

All through the twelve months, there are vows, Brahmin feasts, weddings, thread ceremonies, and calls to perform shraddha. For the great festivals—aradhana, the anniversary of Tikaacharya, and so on—they travel thirty miles to the matha for the communal meal. Thus, the life of the Brahmins flows on in harmony.

This agrahara is called Durvasapura. There is an ancient legend behind the name. In the middle of the flowing Tunga river, at the foot of a small island, stands a hill thickly entwined with trees. It is believed that Durvasa once performed penance there. In the Dvapara Yuga, a special event took place. Ten miles from here, in Kaimara, the five Pandavas spent some time in exile. One day, Draupadi longed to swim in the river. Bhimasena, who fulfilled all her wishes, dammed the Tunga for her.
That morning, the sage Durvasa was preparing for his ritual bath and sandhya...
**Samskara 17**

They rise to look for the Nandanadi and other sacred rivers!—but there is no water at all in the Tunga. They are angered. For Dharmaja, this immediately shines forth as a divine vision, and he advises Bhimasena accordingly. Ever obedient to his elder brother’s word, the son of Vayu breaks the bund he himself had built in three places and lets the water flow. Even today, in the Kayimara, the river splits and flows in three streams from that bund. The Brahmins of Durvasapura tell the Brahmins of the neighboring agraharas: on the morning of Dwadashi, it is believed that the sound of the conch is heard from the Durvasa forest for the pious souls. But none of the agrahara Brahmins ever display the impertinence to claim they have actually heard it.

Thus, from the sthala purana: ever since the great ascetic, the jnani, the Vedanta-shiromani Praneshacharya came and settled here; and because of the outcaste Narayanappa, the fame of the agrahara had spread in all ten directions. To hear the Acharya’s purana, Brahmins from neighboring agraharas would crowd in during festivals like Ramanavami. For Praneshacharya, Narayanappa was a great problem. While serving his ailing wife, striving to justify the mercy of God, he patiently swallowed Narayanappa’s misdeeds, and, by explaining the meaning of mantras filled with incomprehensible words, he tried to dispel the darkness clouding the Brahmins’ minds, gently prodding them towards the fragrance of true grihastha-dharma...

Meanwhile, the Brahmins, their heads covered with angavastra, weak with hunger, walked along the agrahara street, baked to the point where rice would burst open if dropped, crossed the Tunga river at the three streams, entered the cool forest, and after an hour’s walk, reached Parijatapura. The earth, heated by the sun, was not cooled by the green wind of the areca gardens. In the burning dust, the Brahmins’ bare feet were scorched and pricked. Chanting the name of Narayana, the Brahmins entered the house of the moneylender Manjayya—a house they had never set foot in before.
Samskara

The shrewd moneylenders, seated and recording accounts, remarked: “Oh ho ho, what a crowd of Brahmins! It’s been a while since so many feet have gathered here. Oh ho ho, welcome, please sit, let’s ease your fatigue, wash your feet. She—bring some plantains for them…” With such customary hospitality, they spoke. The wife brought fruit on a tray, said “Please have some,” and went inside. Garudacharya, with a sigh, sat down and revealed the news of Narayanappa’s death.

“Ayyo Bhagavan—what happened to him? Just eight or ten days ago he was here on business, said he’d go to Shimoga and return. Asked if I had any work for him. I told him, ‘Come if you hear areca nuts are being sold in the mandi.’ Shiva, Shiva… He said he’d be back by Thursday… Was it some illness?”
“Just four days of fever, that’s all—then the plague, it seems,” said Dasacharya.

“Shiva, Shiva,” Manjayya closed his eyes and fanned himself anxiously. He had often traveled to Shimoga, and the dreadful two-syllable name of the disease came to his mind, but he was afraid to utter it aloud—“Shiva, Shiva,” he repeated.
Within moments, all the Brahmins from the side row of Parijatapura gathered on the veranda.

“You all know,” Garudacharya, firm in affairs, said, “there was a quarrel between the agrahara and him—no food or water passed between us. You all were his friends, weren’t you? Now, with the question of his funeral rites upon us, what shall we do…?”

The people of Parijatapura were grieved by the loss of a friend; yet, at the same time, there was a certain satisfaction that the occasion for the funeral rites of a high-caste Brahmin had arrived. Narayanappa had always been a restless presence in their midst…
Samskara 19
The very fact that he would eat with them was half the reason for their affection toward him.
Shankarayya, the priest for the Brahmins of Parijatapura, spoke:

“According to Brahminical law, even a serpent is called a dvija. That is, if one comes across the corpse of a snake, it must receive the proper samskara; otherwise, it is forbidden to eat. In such circumstances, when a Brahmin is rendered helpless by fate, it is not right for us to simply sit with folded hands. What do you all say?”
He spoke thus to show that he too knew the shastras, that they were not inferior to the Madhvas, to humble their pride.
This caused Durga Bhatta great anxiety: this simple Brahmin, in his rashness, would bring disgrace upon the Smartas themselves, he thought, and spoke with a twist in his words:

“Very well, agreed. Praneshacharya too says the same. But the dilemma before us is this: having consumed meat and liquor, and having thrown the sacred Saligrama into water, is Naranappa truly a Brahmin or not? Who among us is prepared to risk the corruption of our caste? Yet, I fully agree that for a Brahmin’s corpse to remain uncremated is adharma.”
Shankarayya’s heart thudded with fear. Already looked down upon as inferior, he could not bear the thought that his actions would bring further disrepute upon his people:

“If that is so—no, no, we will not act rashly. Among you is Praneshacharya, renowned in the south. Let him tell us, knowing well the dharma of emergencies and the subtlety of righteousness. We are ready, without doubt, to perform Naranappa’s samskara, his Vaikuntha-samaradhane.”
Manjayya said, “There’s no need to worry about expenses. Was he not my friend?”
chapters.summary: Praneshacharya consults ancient scriptures while the Brahmins of Durvasapura debate the proper funeral rites for Narayanappa amidst concerns about gold and religious caste purity.

chapters.title: Memory and Defiance
paragraphs: Samskara
“I myself will arrange for the donations and other rituals,” he said, pricking the miserly Madhva with these words.
# Chapter Three

After all the Brahmins had set off to Parijatapura, Praneshacharya, moved by compassion, told Chandri, “Sit down,” and went to the dining house where his wife lay resting. “She—Chandri—has such a pure heart, you know,” he thought, recalling how she had given the gold, and the new problem that had arisen from it. He spread out the palm-leaf manuscripts and books, searching for what the Dharma Shastra prescribed in such a situation. Narayanappa had always been a problem for him. In the agrahara, would it be his own asceticism, holding fast to Sanatana Dharma, that would ultimately prevail, or Narayanappa’s demonic nature? That was his stubborn question. He grieved, wondering what evil fate had made Narayanappa turn out this way, and, praying for God’s mercy to redeem him, he fasted two nights a week, leaving aside his meal. Besides, the reason his heart was so full of remorse and anxiety for Narayanappa was the promise he had made to Narayanappa’s mother: “I will look after your son’s welfare, I will bring him to the right path”—thus he had comforted the dying old woman. But Narayanappa had not come to the right path; he had not heeded any words of wisdom. The son of Garuda, Shyama, whom he had taught the Vedas and made recite mantras by heart, and Lakshmana’s son-in-law, Shripati—he had drawn both away from his own influence. He had encouraged Shyama to leave home and join the military. After hearing endless complaints brought by Garuda and Lakshmana, Praneshacharya had finally gone to see Narayanappa one day. Narayanappa, lying on a thin mattress, showed just enough respect to rise and sit up when he saw Praneshacharya. But when he tried to offer advice—

He spoke whatever came to his mind. He derided Brahminical dharma: “Your shastras have no place anymore. The Congress is coming. Panchamas must be allowed into the temple,” he rambled incoherently. I wondered, should I care? Should I not have separated that Shripati from his wife? He laughed aloud. “Who would marry a girl who brings no happiness, Acharya, except these foolish Brahmins?” he mocked. “Why should I tie a mad girl to myself and ruin her life? You Brahmins—let your dharma be yours. Life is but a span. I am of the Charvaka lineage—‘R̥ṇam kṛtvā ghṛtam pibet’—incur debt, but drink ghee,” he declared. He taught: “This physical body is not eternal.” He pleaded: “Do what you will, but at least do not ruin the lives of girls.” He gestured helplessly. Even at that, he laughed. “Is a Brahmin, according to you, one who grabs the property of the shaven-headed, who performs sorcery, who drives away evil with spells?” he ridiculed. “In the end, who will win, you or I? Let us see, Acharya. How long do you think this Brahminhood will last? If I wish, I can throw all the honor of Brahminhood into the dust for the pleasure of a woman. Now go. I do not wish to speak further and hurt you,” he said.

Why did I stand in the way of excommunicating such a man? Was it fear? Was it remorse? Or a stubbornness that I would win in the end? In any case, as he was in life, so he is now in death—testing the very essence of my Brahminhood.

The last time I saw Naranappa was three months ago, on the evening of a Chaturdashi. That morning, he had taken some Muslims with him, caught the sacred fish from the Ganapati temple’s river, and, holding the deity’s honor in his hands, paraded it before all in the agrahara, so Gurudacharya complained. He came upstairs, ate rice with his hands, and played in the river with those great fish that swam there.
Samskara

Praneshacharya was alarmed that Narayanappa had disregarded the belief that those who touch the untouchables would die a bloody death: now that he had set such an example, would not everyone, one by one, stray from the path of justice and dharma, becoming shudras and worse? Even in this age of Kali, it was only the fear of the divine that preserved some sense of righteousness among the common people. If even that were to be destroyed—where else would the power remain to uphold this earth? Now, to remain silent was utterly improper, he felt, and so, heart pounding, he strode straight to Narayanappa’s face and stood in the latter’s quarters.
He seemed to have been drinking: his eyes were bloodshot, his hair disheveled...
And—had he not, on seeing Praneshacharya, suddenly risen and covered his mouth with his garment?

At times, the Acharya, lamenting that Narayanappa’s nature was like a chakravyuha—an impenetrable maze—felt there was perhaps no way for him to enter it. Yet now, seeing a crack in that arrogant Ravana-like pride, seeing that Narayanappa was at least startled by his presence, a hope blossomed within him, as if a gentle, sattvic power had begun to flow from within.

He knew now that words would be useless. Unless the sacred Ganga waters of his own inner purity could silently flow into Narayanappa’s heart, he would never be transformed. A desire arose in him, fierce as longing, to swoop down like Garuda, shatter Narayanappa’s shell, and draw forth the nectar within.

He gazed at him sternly. He looked at him as one would look at an ordinary sinner, expecting him to tremble, to shrink, to be humbled—just so. If only two drops of repentance would fall from his eyes, that would suffice. Narayanappa, five years younger than himself, he wished to embrace and forgive with brotherly affection—if only he would relent.
Narayanappa lowered his head. Like Garuda swooping down in a rush—
Samskara 23
Like someone who has found a beginning, like a momentary thrill, like peeking through a half-opened door and being struck with wonder—he saw...
No. He pulled the cloth from his mouth, flung it onto the chair, and laughed harshly:
"Chandri, where is the bottle? Give the Acharya some tirtha."
"Close your mouth!" Praneshacharya, trembling all over, saw him, stripped of all restraint, and as he tried to swallow his anger, he felt as if he had missed a step and was left desolate.

"Ah! So even the Acharya can get angry? I thought lust and anger were only for people like us. Even one who has trampled down desire, it seems, still has anger at the tip of his nose... Durvasa, Parashara, Bhrigu, Brihaspati, Kashyapa—Chandri, where is the bottle? Acharya, your rishis were something else. What was the name of the one who made a fragrant woman fragrant by washing her in a boat? Look at these poor Brahmins of the agrahara, descended from such a lineage..."
"Naranappa, close your mouth," I said.

Seeing that Chandri did not bring the bottle, Naranappa grew angry, climbed the stairs to the loft himself, brought down the arrack, and filled a cup. When Chandri tried to stop him, he pushed her away.
Praneshacharya closed his eyes and turned his back, intending to leave.

"Acharya, wait a moment," he said. Fearing that if he left now, he would appear afraid, Praneshacharya stood there mechanically. The smell of arrack was revolting. "Listen," Naranappa commanded, taking a gulp from the cup and smiling crookedly, he said:

"In the end, let’s see who wins—you or I. I will destroy Brahminhood. I will, I swear it. My only sorrow is that in this agrahara there is no Brahminhood left to destroy—except for you. Garuda, Lakshmana, Durgabhatta—ah, what Brahmins they are! If I remain a Brahmin in any way..."
Samskara

“Your Garudacharya would have forced me into compromise. Or, out of greed for property—like Lakshmana, who licks up coins fallen into the gutter with his very tongue—he would have tied another corpse-like woman to me. In short—I would have had to grow my hair, smear ash on my forehead, sit on your platform, and listen to the Puranas you recite...”

Naranappa took another gulp and paused. From inside, Chandri, fear-stricken, stood with folded hands, signaling him to stop. Praneshacharya turned away again—what was the point of arguing with a drunkard?
“Acharya, listen here. Why this pride that the agrahara must always heed your words? Lend an ear to mine as well. Let me tell you a Purana. Listen!

“Once, in an agrahara, there lived a most venerable Acharya—in times long past. His wife was always ill, so he knew nothing of a woman’s pleasure. His brilliance—that is, his fame—spread from village to village. The other Brahmins in the agrahara were utter sinners. They committed every sin born of food and gold. But they believed that, somehow, the Acharya’s merit would cover their sins, so they began to sin even more freely. Thus, as the Acharya’s merit increased, so did their sins.

“One day, something amusing happened. Are you listening, Acharya? The moral of my story is this: for every action we perform, not only do we receive its proper fruit, but also its opposite. Tell this to the other Brahmins as well.

“The amusing thing was, there was a young man in that agrahara. His wife, though married to him, never lay with him—out of obedience to her mother’s words. Every evening, that young man would attend the Acharya’s Purana recitation. For, though he had no experience in life, the Acharya was a true connoisseur of poetry and music.
Samskara 25

One day, there was a reading of Kalidasa’s Shakuntala. This young man, weary of the wife who, at the slightest touch, would run to her mother to complain, felt, through the Acharya’s description, as if a woman had sprung up within his own body, as if a fire had been kindled in his loins—do you know what that means, Acharya?—he leapt up from the veranda and ran. Unable to bear listening any longer, he went straight to the river, hoping to lose himself in the cool water. By fortune, there was a farm woman there. Moonlight. By fortune, her body was barely clothed, and all the limbs he longed to see were shamelessly revealed before his eyes. She was like your rishi’s beloved Matsyagandhi. Mistaking her for Shakuntala herself, this Brahmin youth lay with her right there—under the witness of the moon.

“Now, tell me plainly, Acharya: Was it not that Acharya who ruined the Brahminhood of the village—yes or no? That’s why the elders always said: Read the Vedas and Puranas, but don’t try to understand them. Haven’t you been to Kashi yourself? You tell me: Who corrupted Brahminhood?”
Listening to Narayanappa’s words, standing motionless, Praneshacharya was troubled: Was this the drunken rambling of a madman? Or was it true? Could such a transgression be possible from himself?
“Virtue has no tongue, but sin does,” Praneshacharya sighed. “May God show you mercy—that is all I can say.”

“You read the Puranas with relish, but you teach people to live like fools. But my words have only one meaning: to sleep with a woman is to sleep with a woman; to eat meat is to eat meat. Shall I give you a piece of advice, Acharya? First, push your own sick wife into the river. Then, like the rishis of the Puranas, embrace a Matsyagandhi who can give you real pleasure, and lie with her. When you open your eyes and see—”
chapters.summary: Praneshacharya searches ancient scriptures for guidance on the funeral rites while recalling his past confrontation with the defiant and drunken rebel known as Naranappa.

chapters.title: Rites and Rivalries
paragraphs: 26. Samskara
“If you have not experienced the Supreme Being, then my name is not Narayanappa,” he said, winking, and gulped down the liquor in his cup with a noisy swig, then let out a loud “Hey!” as he finished.

Acharya, deeply disturbed at the thought that this man could torment his own ailing wife in such a manner, spat out, “You wretch!” and hurried back home. That night, when he sat for his prayers, he found it impossible to restrain the whirl of thoughts. He grew anxious, repeating “Paramatma, Paramatma…” to himself. Instead of reading the usual evening tales full of flavor and delight, he began to narrate stories of moral conduct and religious vows. The result—his own enthusiasm for reciting the puranas faded away. The boys, whose bright, eager eyes and attentive listening had always brought joy to his heart, stopped coming. Only the widows and elders, those who sought to accumulate merit, who would belch and murmur the Lord’s name in the middle of the story, continued to attend.

Sitting in the hall, reading palm-leaf manuscripts and lost in thought, Praneshacharya noticed his wife groaning in pain. Realizing he had not yet given her the afternoon medicine, he brought the medicine on a plate, lifted her gently, cradled her to his chest, and poured the medicine into her mouth. “Lie down and sleep,” he said softly. Returning to the inner room, he stubbornly resumed reading: “If the Dharmashastra gives no answer to this, what does it mean?”
Chapter Four

Meanwhile, from Parijatapura, under the scorching sun and with hunger gnawing at him, someone trudged along, murmuring “Hari, Hari,” hoping to find some rest in his own home. But among the Brahmins, the council of their wives had already begun—chiefly with Garudacharya and Lakshmanacharya at the center.
Garudacharya’s only son, Shyama, had run away from home and joined the military, for reasons that were the subject of much speculation.
Samskara 27.

In the agrahara, they say: unable to bear his father’s punishment, he left. If it is Garudacharya, they say, “If it is Narayanappa, everyone who saw him was inspired by him to join the military.” Moreover, even after learning lessons from Praneshacharya, if he was to act with such wickedness and run away—Lakshmanacharya’s opinion is that the spell Garuda had cast on Narayanappa’s father has now turned back upon Garuda himself. Like Bhasmasura, who tried to burn his own creator, these spells and mantras have now recoiled. Had Garuda not performed the spell, “Why should Narayanappa, born in a noble family, become a chandala like this?”—so lamented Anasuya, Lakshmanacharya’s wife, grieving that a stain had come upon her mother’s lineage.

Because of the chandala Narayanappa’s influence, the son they had raised with such care was ruined and ran away—thus, Garudacharya’s wife, Sitadevi, gave up food and water, pined away, waited day and night at the threshold. After three months, a letter came from Shyama—saying he was in Pune, had joined the military, and that after joining, unless he paid six hundred rupees, he would not be allowed to return. Sitadevi, placing her hand on her waist, stopped Narayanappa on the street and wept, wrote a letter to her son: “Do not eat meat, do not give up your daily bath and sandhyavandana.” On Friday night, she fasted, hoping good sense would return to her son. Garudacharya, seized by Durvasa’s wrath, declared, “He is as good as dead to me. If he sets foot in this house, I will tear him apart,” and raged like one stung by red ants. Sitadevi, praying to Tulasi, pleaded, “Grant my husband some peace, let him keep his love for his son,” and began a vow on Saturday as well.
As if pouring ghee into a burning fire, the Madhva-hater Durgabhatta said, “In the military, there is neither bath nor sandhyavandana—”
Samskara could not be performed; they claimed they were being forced to eat meat, and this had made Garudacharya bow his head in shame.

When Seethadevi returned home, she was elated to find Chandri’s jewelry in her possession, thinking it might help her find a way to get her son released from the military. But according to the Dharmashastra, her husband could not perform the samskara for Naranappa’s corpse. What if Lakshmanacharya agreed before her husband did? Or if the Parijatapura Brahmins, who had no ties to the widow, gave their consent first? She grew restless. She made a vow to Maruti, offering fruits and coconuts—“Oh Lord, let my husband be the one to perform the samskara.”

Now, in her eyes, Naranappa’s eating of meat no longer seemed such a terrible sin. What if, tomorrow, her own son returned home, and the tongues of injustice in the agrahara began to wag against him too? What would become of him if he were excommunicated? She, who had once complained about Praneshacharya for not taking the lead in excommunicating Naranappa, now remembered him with respect: he is compassionate; surely, he would take her son’s sins upon himself and offer guidance—there was no doubt.

As soon as she returned home, she lay down on the floor and wept. Garudacharya, seeing her distress, said, “To me, he is as good as dead. Don’t even mention that wretch’s name.” Yet his wife’s words clung to him like a burr. Let everything be destroyed, let even his son perish, but he was not prepared to destroy his own Brahminhood. But if Praneshacharya were to give his assent, everything would be resolved. Only then, after his own death, could his only son perform his funeral rites and be released from the military.

He silenced his wife harshly—“That’s impossible. Keep your mouth shut”—and, like a thief, Garudacharya set out for Praneshacharya’s house. Avoiding Chandri, who sat in the courtyard, he entered directly into the inner part of the Acharya’s home.
Samskara 29
Praneshacharya sat, head bowed, reading the palm-leaf manuscripts:

“Sit down, Garuda. The people of Parijatapura say we should do as the Dharmashastra prescribes. For the record, what they say is correct,” he said, turning the page and continuing to read. Garuda cleared his throat and asked, “What does the Manusmriti say, Acharya...?”
Praneshacharya shook his head.

“What is there in the Dharmashastra that you do not know? That’s not what I meant. Remember that day—what was it—the punyadina of Tikacharya—what was it—you sat in the matha, by the pillar, before the revered Shri Guru, with the great scholars of Vyasaraya Matha—what was it—you debated with them, did I not hear of it? When you interpreted ‘bimbosi, pratibimbosmi’ according to the Madhyamata, the others were left speechless. That day, the meal was delayed by four hours because of the debate. So, you must not think I have come to instruct you. Before you, I am nothing but a Singalika. What am I?”

Seeing Garuda’s attempts to flatter him, to draw him to his side, Acharya felt a wave of distaste. What is or isn’t in the Dharmashastra doesn’t matter to him; he just wants the words to come from my mouth, so that no one can find fault—he knows this, and so he keeps pushing me up onto the dais. The reason: that gold, the fruit of generosity, and its opposite. As Narayanappa said, I must not melt into compassion now. I must stand firm and do as the Dharmashastra commands.
“Is it possible that the rishis, knowers of the three times, did not think of this? What?”
Without answering Garuda, Acharya continued reading.
“The reason it is called Vedanta, what, is that its philosophy is the end—”
Samskara

“Was it not you yourself who once gave such an instruction, Acharya? Is it possible that Vedanta can remain without an answer? When a Brahmin’s corpse lies within the agrahara, and when the Brahmins of the keri are thus prevented from properly observing the rites and rules of their Brahminhood—what then? I am not raising this question merely to ask whether we may eat or not… What is it?”
Praneshacharya did not answer this either. All the Vedanta, Puranas, and philosophy he had once taught—now Garuda was returning them to him. Why? Gold! Ah, the life of man, he thought.

“And besides, what you said seemed true to me. Even if he abandoned Brahminhood, Brahminhood did not abandon him, did it! We never truly excommunicated him, did we? If we had, then he would have become a turuka, and we would have been compelled to leave this agrahara, would we not?”
“My resolve is only to do as the Dharmashastra commands, Garuda,” he said, lifting his eyes from the book to stop Garuda’s words, and then returned to reading.

“If the Dharmashastra does not provide a subsequent answer, let it be so. I am not saying it cannot be found. If, by chance, it cannot be found, is there not such a thing as apaddharma, emergency dharma, which you yourself once spoke of? If, to save a man’s life, one must give him beef, then even beef is not a sin—you yourself have said this, have you not? According to a story you once told, when famine struck the earth, the sage Vishwamitra, unable to bear his hunger, to save his life—which is the highest dharma—even ate the flesh of a dead dog, did he not?”
“I understand, Garuda. Now, tell me what is truly in your mind.”
Samskara 31

With a weary sigh, Praneshacharya closed the palm-leaf manuscripts and asked, “There is nothing, is there, appa?” Garudacharya replied, eyes fixed on the ground. Then, after offering the Acharya a deep, defiant namaskara, he rose and sat up: “If Shyama is not released from the military, who will perform my funeral rites, Acharya? If I could get your permission, then…” He trailed off, as if about to say more, when Lakshmanacharya arrived and stood there.

Anasuya, Lakshmanacharya’s wife, who had returned home weeping, believed the ornament that should have adorned her sister’s neck had been lost, and that her sister had died because of this misfortune. Gradually, her tears began to flow for Narayanappa as well. After all, was he not her own uncle’s son? If her uncle had lived, if her sister had survived, if that Garuda had not performed his black magic, would their Narayanappa have lost his mind like this, pawned so much gold, and died like a destitute stranger, left to rot without funeral rites? The thought made her sob. “Whatever he did, the bonds of the heart cannot be severed, O Lord,” she cried, pressing her face to the wall. But the very next moment, her heart turned to stone as she saw her daughter Leelavati, hair tightly braided, nose-ring shining, a long streak of vermilion on her forehead, circling the grinding stone in the kitchen. “How many times must I ask—did Shripati say when he would return?” For the tenth time, she asked. Leelavati replied, “I don’t know.” Had she, by giving her daughter in marriage to that foreign boy, driven her own Narayanappa mad? Was she, like a serpent that devours its own eggs, the cause of her own suffering? What more misfortune would befall her son-in-law? In the house…
Samskara

He does not stay even two days in a month. He wanders from village to village, following the Yakshagana troupes. He keeps company with the boys of Parijatapura. Word has reached her, through Durga Bhatta’s wife, that he has mistresses here and there. Only when she secretly visited Shripati after he had returned from Narayanappa’s house did she realize—he has gone astray. He has taken the wrong path. Fate! Who knows what he ate and drank there! None can resist the allure of that Chandri. To teach her son-in-law a lesson, Anasuya instructed her daughter: “Do not yield to your husband. Tie your thighs together and sleep curled up like a conch. Let him come to his senses.” Leelavati did exactly that. When her husband came to her at night, she would begin to cry, “He’ll burn, he’ll bite,” and go to sleep in her mother’s room.

It did not seem that Shripati learned any lesson from this. She could not now manage her husband’s desires as she once had. Shripati shaved his head and grew a stubble like Narayanappa. With the money he had collected as dakshina, he bought a battery. In the evenings, he began to blow a whistle and walk around the agrahara. Already emaciated by fever, his eyes sunken, Lakshmanacharya looked as if he might die any day. Now, from the sun and hunger, he became even more skeletal, and collapsed at home. Immediately, Anasuya began to haunt him: Wasn’t her maternal uncle’s son Narayanappa? Whatever disgrace he brought upon the lineage, if his woman had been carried away by Shudras, she would not have survived it. Praneshacharya’s nature is gentle. Garuda is not like you simpletons—he is fierce, powerful, capable of destroying a whole village. If he somehow gets permission to perform the samskara for the corpse, all the ornaments, already spinning with pride, will go to Sita Devi. Let God do what is fitting for their wicked minds. Otherwise, Shyama will run away from home and join the military.

Am I joining them? Now they say—about my son-in-law, my maternal uncle’s son, Naranappa—that his son Shyama Acharya is carrying on the family tradition. But what proof is there of that? Don’t let Garuda go alone to win over Praneshacharya’s mind. You go too. He’s there now—while you’re sitting here, struck by penance—don’t I know? she said, stepping outside and forcefully driving her husband out, inspecting the front and back of Garudacharya’s house.

In the midst of Shiva worship, the sight of the ragged, beggarly Lakshmanacharya made Garudacharya furious beyond measure. Hissing with anger, clutching his protruding belly with one hand, and digging the earth with the other, he glared at the man sitting there as if he would swallow him whole. Praneshacharya, who stood before him, suppressed the urge to call him all the names—miser of misers, chief among the stingy, henpecked husband. This Brahmin, hard-fisted as a thunderbolt, would not accept even a spoonful of sesame oil for an offering. Who in the agrahara does not know? If his wife nags him to buy oil, he rises at dawn and walks four miles to the Konkani shop. “Well, Kamath, how did you get such good oil? What’s the price? How’s the stock? Is it fresh? Let me see,” he says, stretching out his hand for two spoonfuls, pretending to sniff and taste it, and then, as if unconcerned, “No worries. Still, Kanayya, tell me when the new stock comes in, our house needs a tin,” and strokes it over his head. Then, dipping his hand into the sack of chillies, “What’s the price for a maund?” he asks, and, chatting amiably, slips a fistful of chillies into his own bag. From there, he walks another mile straight to Shenoy’s shop: “At Kamath’s shop...

“How expensive it is!”—thus cursing the merchant, she bought two more spoonfuls of sesame oil, a handful of chilies. Returning home, she bathed, cooked. Again, she went to their garden, cut banana leaves, dried them, made plates, sold them, and earned a little money. She sold her sacred thread for a little more. She waited for the call to eat like a hawk. Now, his eyes are set on the gold. Whatever happens, he must not get it.

“Narayana, Narayana,” sighed Lakshmanacharya, wiping his sweat, “Acharya, if there is no prohibition in the Dharmashastra, I have no objection to performing the samskara for the corpse. After all, he is of my own shadkaksha. If you permit, the right to perform the samskara belongs to me and no one else.” He opened his eyes, which had been closed in thought.

Garudacharya was annoyed. What weapon did he have against this? “If the question is about the eligibility to perform the samskara—well—there is nothing stopping me. Let him do it. After all, was a Brahmin birth given for anything but to accept the sins of others? But that gold must go to the court. Or, according to the justice of Dharmasthala, it should come to me.”

Praneshacharya was deeply troubled. Even if the question of the corpse’s samskara were resolved, the question of the gold would not be so easily settled. With every passing moment, his responsibility grew heavier. Narayanappa’s challenge was growing into a Trivikrama. Just then, the poor Brahmins, led by the impoverished Dasacharya, joined them.

“Acharya…” Dasacharya, rubbing his stomach as a mother soothes the back of a crying child, said, “My health is not good—you know that. If I go without food, my very life is in danger. You must show us a way. Or else, in this calamity—”

If anything is to be done according to the rules, an order must be given. Tell us, is it possible to eat while the corpse remains in the agrahara? Moreover, this is the height of summer; within another day, the stench of the corpse will surely begin to spread. My house is close to his. This is not good for anyone. For the welfare of the agrahara, Lakshmanacharya or Garudacharya must come to a decision.”
He stopped speaking and looked around. Just as Narayanappa was driven by desire, Dasacharya was driven by hunger. Hunger saved him at this moment. It lent him a certain wisdom, made him speak:

“If you decide, Acharya, that is enough. Your word is as the word of the Veda. We do not want gold—we want nothing. You command. We four will at once lift the corpse, carry it away, and perform the samskara. That gold—let it be used to make a crown for Maruti in service to him.”

Within Praneshacharya, a sudden surge of sattvic energy stirred. Garudacharya and Lakshmanacharya, however, were disheartened. Garudacharya, summoning all his stubbornness, pondered what ought to be said in such a situation. To oppose Dasacharya’s suggestion that the gold be offered to Maruti would be a great sin. So, what could he say now?

“Let the Acharya do as the Dharmashastra prescribes. There will always be those who object. But if the Acharya acts rashly—if, somehow, the Gurus deem it a transgression—what then? What will become of us all? We must ensure, above all, that the Acharya’s reputation is not tarnished. What if, as the people of Parijatapura were ostracized, the Brahmins everywhere cast us out...?”
So, Garudacharya, smiling gently, spoke as if he agreed with Dasacharya, though he was only pretending. From this...
chapters.summary: Praneshacharya seeks guidance from ancient scriptures while Garudacharya and the other Brahmins debate the religious implications of performing a controversial funeral for their rival.

chapters.title: Night's Forbidden Crossing
paragraphs: Samskara
Even Lakshmanacharya, who did not understand what the gardener had said, felt relieved.
“Now all of you go home, Acharyas. I will turn over all the Dharma Shastras from their roots and find an answer to this—tonight itself, sitting up,” said Praneshacharya, deeply troubled.

Evening fell. But there was no sandhyavandana, no meal. Praneshacharya, with nothing to do, wandered restlessly from inside to outside, from outside to inside. He called out to Chandri, who was sitting in the courtyard, “Come up and sit here.” He lifted his wife in both arms, as if she were a child, carried her to relieve herself, then brought her back and laid her on the bedding. He gave her the evening medicine, then returned to the central room and sat turning the pages of the shastras in the light of the lantern.
Chapter Five

The previous night, Shrinalli had gone to see the Jambuvanti-Kalyana of the Keluru troupe. Shripati, who had returned, did not know that Narayanappa had come from Shimoga and was lying in bed, nor that he had died. Had he known, the secret grief of losing a close friend would have troubled him throughout the agrahara. It had been a week since he had left home. Befriending the Bhagavata of the Keluru troupe, he had wandered with the players, staying with them, eating with them, watching the play at night, sleeping during the day, and in his spare time, going to the neighboring villages to invite people, offering betel leaves to welcome the troupe.
Samskara 37

For a week, lost in lively and skillful conversation, he had forgotten the world. But tonight, holding a battery torch in his hand, he walks through the darkness of the forest, uttering a brave word now and then to steel his courage. The hair on his shaven crown, grown untended down to his neck, is because the Bhagavata had promised him a female role next year. After all, was it not Praneshacharya who had refined his tongue? The Bhagavata had praised him, saying, “Your speech flows pure from your throat.” Besides, from the Acharya he had heard some Sanskrit logic and Puranic tales, and so he possessed the culture necessary for the profound dialogues of Yakshagana. Once he had secured a part in the troupe, Sripati was filled with joy, thinking he could escape the Brahmin herd that lived only for fat rice, sweet payasa, and the fleshy bulbs of jackfruit. In the darkness of the forest, he felt no fear.

Moreover, the heady toddy he had drunk in Pujari Sheena’s hut had risen warmly to his head, so the deep silence of the forest did not make him tremble. Two bottles of toddy; a battery torch that, at the press of a button, spread light—a wondrous thing for the village folk—thus armed, what need had he to fear ghosts or spirits? As he neared Durvasapura, his body grew warm with the anticipation of pleasure awaiting him. What if his wife tied her thighs in a knot and slept curled up? She would be there in the morning. What if she grew dark? Didn’t Narayanappa say—what if she turned black? What if she became bald? She was neither black nor bald. Which Brahmin girl, with her hidden gums, shriveled breasts, and mouth smelling of lentil stew, could compare to her? What did he lack in Belli, who filled his hands and thighs, who slithered beside him in sand and mud like a snake? By now, she would have bathed in the hot water kept in the pot before the hut, drunk enough of her father’s sour toddy to be warm and mellow—like the mridanga after tuning. Not pitch black, nor faded white—
Samskara

Her skin bore the color of earth baked in the tender, fertile sunlight that ripens the seed. Shreepati’s footsteps halted. For his own amusement, he flicked on the battery torch, casting its beam and then letting it die. Again he switched it on, sweeping the light around the forest, swelling with pride like an actor entering in a demon’s guise. Thaithai takathai—thaithai: he danced. He tried to spin a brass plate on his knee, curious to see if it would whirl, but it struck his knee and he sprang up. The solitude of the forest, the flutter of birds startled by the torchlight, only intoxicated him further. At his call, the nine rasas assembled: wrath, disgust, fury, devotion, erotic love—his imagination slipped seamlessly from one to another. Now, in the half-light, Lakshmidevi, in the cadence of Yakshagana, sang a hymn to Shesha-shayi that would not see the dawn...
Awaken... Narayana Awaken, consort of Lakshmi Awaken, O Lord, the day has broken...

Tears welled in Shreepati’s eyes. Garuda came, circling to rouse him—“Awaken, Narayana.” Narada arrived, strumming his tambura, urging—“Awaken, consort of Lakshmi.” All the beasts and birds, vanaras, kinnaras, yakshas, gandharvas, pleaded—“Awaken, O Lord, the day has broken.” Shreepati, in a dance of lasya, gathered his dhoti like a sari, waving his arms, craning his neck, and danced. Sheena’s wife had already crossed the line—she should go to Narayanappa and cross it further, she thought. The female roles of Yakshagana came to mind. In the puranas, there is not a single rishi who has not succumbed to a woman’s allure. Menaka, who broke Vishwamitra’s penance—how must she have been? Surely more beautiful than the moon. It was a wonder that such a radiant form, coming to gather dung with a rag over her face, escaped the gaze of every eye. Among them...
Samskara 39

No wonder, you might say. What could those dull Brahmin eyes ever see? Again and again, Praneshacharya explains to the children: how ecstatic Vyasa must have been! When he rose at dawn and beheld Ushas, when the Lord made these words flow from his lips—"having bathed, her thighs are like those of Pushpavati, pure and radiant"—ah, what a bold imagination, what a beautiful simile. But to the Brahmins, it is just a mantra, a means to a livelihood.

Look at Kundapura Nagappa, who dons the king’s costume and speaks with such relish: these beetles, these parijata, sampige, mallige, kedage blossoms, this forest grown wild, and you, lonely lady, appearing forlorn, stricken with sorrow—who are you?

Shripati walks by, smiling to himself. In the whole agrahara, only two possess eyes that can truly see beauty: Narayanappa and Chandri. If there is a true embodiment of beauty, it is Chandri. Show me such a figurine anywhere in this hundred-mile expanse—I will concede defeat. Even Durgabhatta is not wholly devoid of appreciation, but his capacity does not extend beyond furtively brushing a Shetty woman’s breast. If you look closely, the true connoisseur is Praneshacharya. Such men are one in a thousand. Every evening, as he recites the Purana and explains the verses with such charm, even the greatest of Bhagavatas would be put to shame. What graceful speech, what gentle laughter, what captivating presence. The way he wears his hair, the sacred ash, the grains of akshata, the zari shawl—none can carry them as he does. In all the eight mathas, among the great scholars of the South, he has debated and returned victorious—he owns fifteen zari shawls, they say. Yet he is not one to flaunt them. Alas, his wife is ever-ailing—no children, no family. When he describes Kalidasa’s portrayals of women with such delight, does he not feel desire himself?
Was it not he who first took Belli to the river, to teach her the ways of the water?
Samskara

Listening to the Shakuntala recited by the Acharya, unable to restrain herself, she rose and left. Filling a pot with water, balancing it atop her head, the end of her worn sari slipping, her clay-colored breasts swaying in the moonlight as she walked—she appeared just like Shakuntala herself. The Acharya’s description seemed to come alive before his eyes.

Shripati walked along the inner path, heading straight towards the hill where the Holaya settlement lay. On the pitch-black night of the new moon, he saw a hut on the hill catch fire and burn. In the flickering light, shadowy forms moved about. He stood at a distance, watching, waiting. No one seemed to be making any attempt to put out the fire engulfing the hut. Astonished, he paused at the fork of a lane and waited. The hut, built of bamboo and thatched with dry leaves, caught fire quickly in the summer heat and was reduced to ashes in moments. The shadowy figures returned to their own huts. Birds, startled by the sudden blaze, left their nests and circled anxiously, crying out, before returning to their homes. Shripati walked softly, stopping a little distance from Belli’s hut, and clapped his hands.

After bathing her head with hot water, wearing only a ragged piece of sari, her waist bare, her mass of black hair falling over her back and face, Belli quietly stepped out of her hut and, without a sound, disappeared into the shadows of the thicket. Shripati waited behind a tree until she vanished, then, glancing around to make sure no one was about, went to the spot where Belli had hidden, switched on his torch, and—embraced her, breathing urgently.
“Ayyo, not today, please,”
Belli said—something she had never uttered before. Shripati was surprised. But, paying no heed to her words, he loosened the cloth at her waist.
Samskara 41
"Pilla and his wife—was it a ghost that possessed them, or what story is this? They died today, ayya."
Shripati did not want to speak now. He pulled down the woman who was standing so defiantly.
"Thinking they were all dead, they left the corpse there and set fire to the hut. They just came and died. The closed eyes did not open."

Shripati was irritated. She was rambling on about something, as if she were somewhere far away. After coming all this way in such anxiety, she was chattering about someone’s death. She was not the kind of woman to speak like this at such a time. She was like a crop bowing under the weight of the falling rain...
Belli, putting on her silver anklet—

"Ayya, what a world. I have never seen such a wonder. Why should a rat’s nest come to our temple, where only sacred oil is kept? Is our temple like a Brahmin’s house? Now, like a relative, it comes and settles here. From the burning sun, it comes rolling and spinning, seeking death. When fire catches the temple, it tries to escape with its life and runs into the forest. I have never seen such misery. If it’s a ghost’s doing, call the exorcist and drive it away. Why should a rat come to a hole-digger’s pit, or die suddenly like a broken stick—call the exorcist."

Shripati put on his dhoti, wore his angavastra, took the matchbox from his pocket, struck a match, fitted the battery, and hurried out. Belli was fit only to sleep, not to talk. If she opened her mouth, it was always about ghosts and spirits.

In his haste to see Naranappa, Shripati lifted his dhoti higher and descended the slope. He thought, "Tonight, after drinking arrack, I’ll sleep there, and in the morning, go to Parijatapura to Nagaraja’s house." He stood in front of Naranappa’s house and pushed the door. It was not latched. He thought, "He must still be awake," and entered inside with relief. Switching on the battery torch, he called out, "Naranappa, Naranappa..."
chapters.summary: Intoxicated by theater and toddy, Shripati wanders through the dark forest to meet Belli before discovering an eerie silence at Narayanappa's unlocked house.

chapters.title: Curses and Corruption
paragraphs: He called out. There was no answer. The stench had grown worse; the foul smell that forced one to empty one’s stomach. He climbed the steps in the dark, feeling his way along the familiar stairs, meaning to knock at the door upstairs. As he turned the corner, his bare foot pressed softly, coldly, against something yielding and slick. He recoiled in disgust, switched on his torch, and looked. Ugh! A rat. Its body limp, dead, sprawled across the floor. Flies, disturbed by the torchlight, rose buzzing from its carcass. He hurried up the stairs, switched on the torch again. Why was Narayanappa lying on the floor, wrapped up like that—perhaps he had covered his face with a cloth, he thought, smiling grimly as he pulled at the covering, calling, “Narayanappa, Narayanappa,” and shook him. Again, that cold touch, like when he had stepped on the rat—he withdrew his hand sharply and shone the torch. The sight that met his eyes: eyelids open, sightless, staring. In the circle of torchlight, flies, maggots, stench.
## Chapter Six

In the agrahara, the eldest woman, Lakshmi Devamma, who had passed seventy, flung open the heavy front door with a loud “Dharo!” and called out, “Hey!” She stepped into the street of the agrahara, stood at the crossroads, and again called, “Hey!” Whenever she could not sleep, or when her mind was troubled, she would come out night after night into the agrahara street, wandering three times up and down, from top to bottom and back again, finally stopping in front of Garudacharya’s house. There, she would summon his sons, grandsons, and ancestors, call upon all the gods and deities as witnesses, heap curses upon them with vehemence, then turn back to her house, pull shut the heavy wooden door with a “Dharo!” and lie down to sleep. Especially as new moon and full moon approached, her cursing habit would grow more intense.

The most talked-about subject in the agrahara: her threshold, her temper. Both are spoken of from one end to the other. Her reputation had spread to all the Brahmin agraharas in the four directions. Some called her Avalakshana Lakshmidevamma, the inauspicious Lakshmidevamma, for she was widowed in childhood. If she appeared, mischievous boys and Brahmins would step back four paces and resume their journey, and she would chase them away, waving her stick, cursing them. But no one took her words seriously. The boys called her Hulitegina Lakshmidevamma, Lakshmidevamma of the anthill. Yet she was most famously known as Half-mad Lakshmidevamma.

Her story was a legend: married at eight, widowed soon after. By fifteen, her mother-in-law and father-in-law had died. The agrahara declared her born under an inauspicious star. Before she turned twenty, her own father and mother too passed away, leaving her alone. What then? The little property and jewelry she had were taken over by Garudacharya’s father, who brought her grandmother to his own house and cared for her. All his dealings were of this kind. Narayanappa’s father, too, was not much wiser, and had managed his property in the same way. Thus, for twenty-five years, Lakshmidevamma spent her days. After Garudacharya’s father died, Garuda took charge. His wife was a miser who served half-filled plates. Quarrels broke out between Lakshmidevamma and her, and soon they were at each other’s throats. Husband and wife together threw Lakshmidevamma out. She was pushed to the ruined house of her dead husband. Since then, Lakshmidevamma had lived alone there, in that dwelling.

She went to Praneshacharya with her complaint. He summoned Garuda and admonished him. From then on, Garuda gave her a rupee every month. That money was of no use to her. Thus, she became venomous toward the one who had swallowed her jewels and coins. Occasionally, Praneshacharya...
Samskara
After scolding all the Brahmins of the agrahara and making them give her more rice than anyone else, Lakshmidevamma’s misanthropy only grew with age, rising within her like slow poison.
Lakshmidevamma, stick in hand, stopped before Garudacharya’s house and, as if compelled by fate, began her tirade:
