Suddenly, the sight of crows and the boundary of their cries struck him like a slap to the forehead. When he reached home, his wife’s face was flushed and boiling. “It’s her, it’s her,” he called out. No reply.
Samskara 87

Has the fever risen? How could one touch an outcaste woman? “Tch!”—chiding himself for his own hesitant scruples, he touched her forehead, only to snatch his hand away at once. At a loss, he placed a damp cloth on her brow, then, with uncertainty, pulled aside her covering and examined her body. Beside her, the cot. Was this the fever that had consumed Narayanappa?

He brewed every herb he knew, forced her mouth open, and tried to pour them in. No medicine would go down her throat. What kind of trial was this, he wondered, pacing restlessly. The cawing of crows and the shrill cries of kites grew unbearable, and, as if his mind were whirling in misfortune, he fled to the backyard. He stood there, dazed. He had no sense of time passing. Evening had come. Seeing the crows and kites fly away, he felt a strange relief—yet, feeling guilty for having left his feverish wife alone, he returned to the house by the back door. Panic seized him.

Lighting a lamp, he called, “Is it you? Is it you?” No answer. A wailing began. Then, to his astonishment, his wife let out a piercing scream from the cot—a long, dreadful, rasping cry that seemed to rise from the depths of her throat and brush against his very soul. Acharya trembled, shaken to the core. The sound, like a shriek from a flute, ceased, and suddenly it was as if lightning had flashed and darkness descended. He felt he could not remain there alone.

Before he could understand what he was doing, he ran toward Narayanappa’s house, calling, “Chandri! Chandri!” No answer. He went inside. Darkness. He searched the central hall, the kitchen. No one. He was about to climb the stairs to the upper floor when the thought struck him—there lies the corpse. The same dread he had felt as a boy, before entering a dark room haunted by goblins, now returned, and he fled back to his own house.
He touched his wife’s forehead: it was cold and clammy.
Night after night, carrying a lantern, he would walk to the areca grove, and from there, head toward Subbannacharya’s house, just behind his own.
chapters.summary: Praneshacharya wanders the desolate agrahara alone as the stench of death lingers and he reflects on his changing desires while his wife falls ill.

chapters.title: Greed at the Temple
paragraphs: Samskara

The four Brahmins who had cremated Dasacharya returned, carrying the wet pancha on their heads, chanting “Narayana, Narayana.” They had brought those Brahmins along, carried his wife’s corpse, and set it alight before dawn. Among the Brahmins, someone seemed to murmur within himself, “There is yet another corpse in the agrahara that needs its samskara.” To the Brahmins who said, “Tomorrow, this matter will be settled before the Guru,” he replied, “You may leave now.” Watching the blazing flames consume the woman who had been his companion in this land of penance, he did not try to hold back his tears; he wept until all his exhaustion was washed away.
Chapter Six

Until the ritual meal was over, the Brahmins kept silent, for it was inauspicious to speak of misfortune. They received tirtha from the Swami, and then finished their meal of delicacies, rice, and payasa. As the Guru had given only a single coin as dakshina to each, Lakshmanacharya was disappointed—“How miserly these ascetics are,” he muttered, clutching his waist. No children, no family, yet they cling to money as to life itself. After the meal, the Brahmins sat on the cool cement floor of the matha’s courtyard, while the Swami, clad in saffron, with tulsi beads around his neck, and a smear of sacred ash and turmeric on his brow, sat on a chair among them, like a doll carved from blood-red sandalwood, rubbing his tiny feet together, and began to inquire after their welfare: “Why didn’t Praneshacharya come? How is he? Is he well? What, he couldn’t send word?”
Garudacharya adjusted his throat and conveyed the grave matter from its roots.
The guru listened to everything with composure and, as if there was not the slightest doubt, said:

“Even if he abandoned his Brahminhood, Brahminhood has not abandoned him. Therefore, performing the funeral rites (samskara) is the proper and rightful duty. But expiation for the transgression must also be done. For that reason, all his property—silver and gold—must go to Lord Krishna of the Srimatha.”
Garuda, gathering courage, wiped his face with his angavastra and said:
“Acharya, you know well the dispute that existed between me and his father. Of the three hundred areca trees in his garden, rightfully, I should have...”
Lakshmanacharya interrupted, saying, “Acharya, shouldn’t there be some justice in this? As you know, Narayanappa’s wife and the woman in my house are sisters...”
Suddenly, anger flashed across the round, reddish face of the Swami:

“What kind of low people are you! Since ancient times, it has been the rule that the property of the orphaned must go to the service of God. Remember, if we do not grant you permission to perform his funeral rites, you will have to leave the agrahara altogether,” he thundered.

Realizing their mistake, the two Brahmins apologized and, along with the others, bowed before the Swami. They looked around for Gundacharya, who had come with them, but he was nowhere to be seen. Upon inquiry, they learned that he, stricken with fever and without having eaten, had lain down on the attic of the matha.
Since there was urgency in performing the funeral rites, the Brahmins left Gundacharya there and set out along the village road.

After his wife’s funeral rites were completed, the Acharya did not return to the agrahara. The fifteen silk shawls with golden borders in his trunk, the two hundred rupees he had saved, the tulsi-bead rosary strung with the gold given by the matha—all these did not even enter his thoughts. He simply walked on, wherever his feet led him, clad in the same clothes, moving eastward, as if surrendering himself to the direction of fate.
chapters.summary: While Garudacharya and the Brahmins seek the Swami's guidance on the funeral rites, greed and religious law collide during a tense temple meeting.

chapters.title: The Wanderer Unbound
paragraphs: The agrahara was shrouded in a heavy silence. The morning sun, usually so eager to slip through the narrow lanes, seemed hesitant today, as if it too was weighed down by the uncertainty that gripped every household. The air was thick with the scent of burning ghee lamps and the faint, lingering aroma of yesterday’s incense, now mingled with the musty odor of fear.

Praneshacharya sat in his small, dimly lit room, his eyes fixed on the sacred texts spread before him. The words, once so clear and comforting, now swam before his vision, elusive and ambiguous. He had spent the night in restless contemplation, searching for guidance in the shastras, but the answers he sought seemed to recede further with every page he turned.

Outside, the agrahara’s elders had gathered again beneath the ancient peepul tree. Their voices, usually so resolute, were now hushed and uncertain. Garudacharya, his forehead smeared with fresh vibhuti, spoke first. “Acharya, what is to be done? The body of Naranappa still lies in his house. The crows have begun to gather. If we do not perform the samskara soon, the pollution will spread.”

Praneshacharya did not answer immediately. He felt the weight of their gazes, the burden of their expectations. He knew that every man present looked to him for a decision, for a way out of this impasse. Yet, within him, doubt gnawed relentlessly.

He remembered Naranappa’s mocking laughter, the way he had flouted every rule, eaten fish with the outcastes, brought a courtesan into his home. And yet, Naranappa was a Brahmin by birth. Was it dharma to deny him the last rites? Or was it a greater sin to pollute the agrahara by performing them for an outcast in spirit?
The women watched from behind the half-closed doors, their faces pale with anxiety. Children, sensing the tension, played quietly, their usual shrieks subdued.

Praneshacharya closed his eyes. He tried to recall the teachings of his guru, the wisdom of the ancient rishis. But the words that came to him now were not from the scriptures, but from the depths of his own troubled heart.
Is dharma a matter of rules, or of compassion? Is purity preserved by shunning the impure, or by embracing them in their final hour?

He opened his eyes and looked at the elders. “Let us wait,” he said softly. “Let us pray for guidance. The path is not clear. Until then, let no one enter Naranappa’s house. Let us keep vigil and seek the answer together.”
The elders murmured their assent, though uneasily. The day wore on, heavy with indecision. The agrahara held its breath, suspended between the old certainties and the unknown that lay ahead.

The morning sun’s heat fell upon the forest floor in shifting patterns, like rangavalli designs. Praneshacharya, dragging his weary feet, had for a long while lost all sense of direction or purpose. Anxiously, he wondered if the remains of his wife’s body—the fragments of bone that had not been consumed by the flames—would now be picked at by dogs and jackals. He felt a pang of regret that he had not waited long enough to gather them and consign them to the waters. But then he reassured himself: having left everything behind, having cast off all bonds, he owed nothing more to anyone.

He thought, let my feet carry me wherever they will; let me walk on, true to that resolve. He tried to steady his mind, to bring it to a state of calm, to move forward with determination. In the past, whenever his mind became restless, he would focus it by chanting “Achyuta, Ananta, Govinda.” Now, too, he felt the urge to repeat those names. He remembered: “Yoga is the cessation of the movements of the mind.” But then he rebuked himself—“No!”—and warned himself even against the comfort of name-recitation. Let the mind, for now, be like the rangavalli patterns the sunlight draws through the branches—open, unguarded, unshaped.

Let there be light in the sky, shade beneath the trees, patterns on the earth. If fortune allows, and a drop of dew touches, there will be a rainbow. Life must become like the sunlight—nothing more. Pure awareness, pure wonder. Like Garuda, wings outstretched, silent and content, floating in the sky. The feet walk, the eyes see, the ears listen. One must simply be, without expectation. Only then does life reach a state of acceptance. Otherwise, it becomes coarse with longing, twisted, tangled like a worn-out thread.
Kanaka’s mind was pure awareness, pure wonder; that is why he came before his guru and asked: “Where, secretly, shall I eat this banana? Where is God?”
He was always there, wasn’t He! God had become a thread woven into my very speech; but unlike Kanaka, I never felt wonder or awakening—so henceforth, God is forbidden to me.

Once God is set aside, I must also cast off the anxieties of guru-ṛṇa, pitṛ-ṛṇa, deva-ṛṇa—the debts to teacher, father, and deity. That is, I must stand apart from society itself. For this reason alone, I resolved to walk on until I reached the edge of the world, and so I set out, determined. In this pathless forest, I must keep walking thus. If I grow weary, if I hunger, if I thirst—Praneshacharya’s chain of thought suddenly halted. Was I not heading into yet another cave of self-deception? Though I had resolved to walk to the world’s edge, why did I not stray too far, drawn back by the distant sound of a cowherd boy’s flute, the bamboo bells around the cows’ necks? Whatever my resolve, my feet led me closer to human habitation. This is the boundary of my world. This is the limit of my freedom. I cannot live without human company.
It is like the story of the sannyasi’s kaupina: to save his loincloth from being gnawed by mice, he kept a cat; to feed the cat milk, he kept a cow; to tend the cow, he married a wife.

Praneshacharya sat beneath a jackfruit tree. First, I must look at this matter clearly. I must live the rest of my life without self-deception. I must examine myself plainly: Why did I walk away after burning my wife? Because the agrahara was rotting, I found it unbearable to return. This is a reason my whole being accepts: the feeling of disgust and impurity that clung to my very nose. And then? I no longer wished to meet the Brahmins who had once sought my guidance. Why is that? Praneshacharya stretched out his legs, trying to ease his fatigue, seeking clarity in his mind.

They waited. Unseen by them, a calf came and stood beside them. It lifted its muzzle to their neck, sniffed, and breathed warmly. Praneshacharya shivered—a sudden jolt—and turned. Looking into the calf’s plaintive, affectionate eyes, something welled up within him. He stroked the calf’s neck. Lifting its head, inching closer, the calf pressed its quivering, bristling body into his caressing hand, and, delighted, began to lick his ears and cheeks with its soft, rough tongue. The tickle made Praneshacharya rise, and, wishing to play with the calf, he slipped his hand under its neck and made a gentle “uppuppuppu” sound. The calf reared up on its hind legs, shook itself, and, dancing in the sunlight, vanished from sight.

Praneshacharya tried to recall what he had been thinking. Was it not the question—why did I not go back and see the Brahmins?—but his mind would not settle. Hunger gnawed at him; he decided he must go to the nearby village and appease it. Following the hoofprints and the scattered dung of cattle, he wandered through the forest for an hour, until a small wayside shrine appeared. He thought, this is not a Brahmin agrahara. Walking a little further, he sat down at the root of a tree at the edge of the village.

The sun was climbing, and even in the shade of the tree, thirst tormented him. He hoped that if a gowda happened to see him, he might bring him some milk or fruit. As he watched, a gowda driving his buffaloes to the tank noticed him, raised his hand in greeting, and came closer. His mouth was full of betel, he spat out a thick red stream, and, with a square cloth tied around his head, he looked to Praneshacharya like the village headman. Meeting a stranger whom he did not recognize brought the gowda a sense of satisfaction.

Because his mouth was full, the Gowda raised his hand in greeting and asked where he had come from. Had he known that this was Praneshacharya, the Gowda would not have stood there, mouth stuffed with betel, questioning him so unceremoniously. When one sheds both samskara and the ghosts of the past, the world begins to see him as just another wandering beggar. This thought brought Praneshacharya a pang of discomfort. Seeing that Praneshacharya did not answer, the Gowda spat out the betel from his mouth, approached a little more politely, wiped the red stains from his moustache with his cloth, and asked:
“Are you one of those who go from house to house?” he inquired, his tone questioning.

Praneshacharya felt a measure of relief—he had shown respect by not asking a Brahmin, “Where to?” which was considered inauspicious. Yet, uncertain how to reply, he simply gestured vaguely and wiped the sweat from his brow. By God’s grace, the Gowda had not recognized him, and this brought him some peace.
“Are you from down the hill?” the Gowda asked again, curiosity piqued. Praneshacharya, for whom lying did not come easily, could only manage a noncommittal “Yes.”
“There must be people going from house to house for alms,” the Gowda remarked.

At this, Praneshacharya’s head bowed in sudden shame. This Gowda had taken him for a Brahmin who goes about collecting alms. All his radiance and dignity lost, he must now appear to the world as just another wandering beggar. The lesson in humility had begun: bend, yield, let go, he thought, and again replied, “Yes.” It struck him then, as if his freedom now extended only so far as to shape himself into whatever form or personality a stranger’s eyes wished to see.
“There aren’t any Brahmin houses nearby,” the Gowda said, standing there, arms akimbo.
“Ss it so?” said Praneshacharya in an indifferent tone.
“About ten or twelve miles from here, there’s a Brahmin agrahara.”
“Oh…”
“It’s farther by the main road. But if you take the inner path, it’s closer…”
“All right.”

“There’s a well here. I’ll fetch a pot, you can draw water and bathe. I’ll give you rice and lentils. Light the stove, cook, and eat. You must be tired, poor man. If you want to go to the agrahara, let me know. There’s a cart—Sheshappa has come here to a relative’s house. But the cart is empty now. The agrahara is close by… But, from what he said, I don’t know if you’ll want to go to that agrahara. A corpse—three days and three nights, a woman’s corpse lay there, rotting. A Brahmin’s corpse, ugh… Sheshappa said: in the middle of the night, to ask for the corpse to be cremated, that blessed soul’s widow came to Sheshappa’s house. The dead body has no kinsmen, it seems. Ugh… a Brahmin’s corpse, rotting like that? Sheshappa said that when he was coming by cart in the morning, vultures were sitting on the roofs of the agrahara houses…”
The gowda, chewing betel leaves, sat down and continued talking.
When Praneshacharya heard that Sheshappa had come here, his heart thudded. He did not want Sheshappa to see him in this state. If he stayed here any longer, it would be trouble.
“If you could give me a little plantain and milk, I’ll move on,” he said, looking at the gowda.
“That’s no trouble, swami. I’ll bring it this very instant. When a hungry Brahmin is sitting in the village, how can we eat? I’ll give you rice, as I said.”
Samskara

He set off straight away. To Praneshacharya, it felt as if he were sitting on thorns. What if he too, like Sheshappa, fell into someone’s gaze? Shrinking with fear, he looked around, growing small, huddling in on himself. Why had this fear arisen in him, who had left everything behind? He fretted, unable to suppress the anxiety that surged within him.
The Gowda brought a betel leaf plate filled with tambula, and a slice of banana, and placed them before the Acharya.

“At an auspicious hour today, a Brahmin came to our village. Would you say a word for us? I paid a hundred rupees and brought a woman for my son. Since she arrived, he’s been sitting dull and listless, seized by some fit. If you would chant a mantra for us…”

By force of habit, Praneshacharya was about to perform his Brahminical duty, but he reined himself in. Even though he had left everything, society still pressed upon him all the duties natural to a Brahmin. It was not easy to escape this. What should he say now to the Gowda, who had brought milk and fruit with such devotion to a stranger? Should he say he was fallen from tapas? That he was no longer a Brahmin? Or should he speak the truth?

“I cannot chant mantras for you today, sir. I am under impurity from the death of a kinsman,” he said, quickly seizing upon the answer, and spoke it with pride. He drank the milk, returned the plate, tied the banana in his cloth, and stood up.

“If you walk a mile this way, you’ll reach a place called Melige. Today, tomorrow, and the day after, there’s a chariot festival there. If you are received well there…” said the Gowda, chewing betel leaf, as he herded his buffaloes along.
As soon as the Gowda disappeared from sight, Praneshacharya again entered the forest path and walked on. His problem grew heavier.
Samskara 99

He worried, thinking the crisis had truly come upon him. Never before had he experienced such anxiety—a fear that something would be exposed, a fear that nothing could be kept secret from anyone’s eyes. He had lost his earlier fearlessness. How? Why? The main reason he could not return to the agrahara was this very anxiety—the impossibility of living under the gaze of those Brahmins, the dread of carrying a lie in his lap.

As the deep silence of the forest enveloped him, his mind began to clear. Slowly, he walked, peeling and eating bananas. Since seeing the Gowda, the problem had become even more complex. He must seize it by the hair, bring it face to face. At its root was an object that must be burned—Narayanappa, who had trampled Brahminhood underfoot. The problem was this: among things destined one day to be consumed by fire, there was one thing that must be burned. This problem belonged to dharma, so he turned to the shastras. He turned to God. At last, in the darkness of the forest… he stood still, waiting, his mind swinging, hoping to know with certainty.

…But when he tried to recreate what exactly had happened, how it had happened, it felt like chasing a dream. The sudden thrill from the accidental touch of her breasts, the bananas she took from her lap and fed him—hunger, fatigue, the despair born of exhaustion—all were reasons. Unexpectedly, as if by divine will, that moment had come upon him. It was a moment—beyond it, there was nothing; before it, there was nothing. A moment that came into being from nothing and vanished again into nothingness. Beyond it, formlessness. Before it, formlessness. In between, a moment that had taken shape and possessed him. On that day, I am not entirely responsible for having lain with her. That is, I am not responsible for that moment. But that moment changed me—why? Am I now responsible for the changed man I have become?
Samskara

Restlessness? Was it because the moment had become a memory? It arrived unbidden, without expectation. Now it has become a memory—and as I stir that memory, desire begins to awaken again. I feel the urge to seek out Chandri once more.

Desire coursed through Acharya’s body, making his skin ache for touch. His eyes grew misty. He longed to embrace Chandri and leave for Kundapura. The clarity of mind with which he would usually examine himself through reason seemed to falter. If I now go in search of her and unite with her, would I not become wholly responsible for my own act? If, instead, it had happened suddenly, by chance, perhaps I could have escaped the torment of memory. Then I could look the gods in the eye and say: this is me, this is mine, this is the new truth, the new self born from me. But now, my selfhood stands deformed, without a new shape, like a monstrous lump torn hastily from the womb. I must also examine, with utter honesty, my own belief that that moment in the darkness of the forest came upon me by accident. It is true—it happened by accident. It is true—I did not seek it out. Outstretched hands touched her breasts—again, desire arose, again—there lies the secret. That was the moment when my life was to be decided, whether it would turn this way or that. No—it was a moment I could have chosen myself. That my body consented is no comfort; in the darkness, hurried hands searched—Chandri’s soft thighs, her hips—all without searching for any dharma. In that moment, when my life was to be decided one way or the other, the decision to unite with Chandri was made. Even if I lost control, the responsibility for that decision was mine alone. The value of a man’s decision lies in the very possibility of losing control; only then does decision have meaning.
Samskara 101

It is not because of how smoothly one drinks. We shape ourselves through our own resolutions, giving this vessel the outlines of a personality. Just as Narayanappa decided how he wanted to be and lived accordingly, he became that kind of person. I too lived with the resolve to become something else. At a sudden turning, I turned. Until it became clear to me that the responsibility for that turn was mine, there was no freedom. What happened because I turned? Duality entered my life. Between two truths, I became a Trishanku, suspended. I wonder how the rishis faced such experiences in life—did they face them without conflict? When Matsyagandhi sat in the boat and Vyasa was born, did that great soul set out in distress like me? Did Vishwamitra, fallen from his penance, experience this anxiety? Did they, seeing the whole of life as moments of urgent renunciation, always surrender to the Supreme, and by living through conflict, transcend it—enduring all the transformations churned by the earth, flowing on and finally becoming formless in the ocean, like a river? For me, the Supreme has never been such an immediate urgency. If it was, it must have been so for my dearest friend, Mahabala. Only in him did the Supreme become a longing. The two of us went together to Kashi. He was impossibly clever. In his thin, fair, tall frame, there was nothing beyond his mind’s grasp. Even as the teacher began a lesson, he would already have guessed what was to come. For him alone, I felt an impossible envy, a love. Compared to him, whether in form or in intellect, I was always a little behind. I was a Madhva, he a Smarta, but that never stood in the way of our deep friendship. While I stubbornly insisted on upholding the Madhva doctrine, he would say, “For me, the experience of the Supreme is all that matters; everything else is secondary.” The Supreme...
Samskara

Does not experience require a path? If Daitha argued that such a path existed, then was Vaikuntha some distant city or village to be reached by walking upon it? No, he insisted, it must be found right where one stands. More than dialectics or metaphysics, what he cherished was music. When he began to sing Jayadeva the poet’s Gita Govinda, it was as if he were transported to Nandana itself. “Lalita lavanga lata parishilana komala malaya samare”—as memory surged forth, recalling his friend, Praneshacharya’s voice trembled with emotion. O Supreme One—such love, I have not felt in a long time. What became of Mahabala? When I was in Kashi, he drifted far from me. I never understood why. I was plunged into deep sorrow. My studies, my learning, all came to nothing. The one who was always by my side slipped away and began to wander. I never knew the reason. Day and night, I yearned for Mahabala as I had never yearned for anyone else. I was overcome by longing. Looking back over my whole life, I realize that the love I bore for Mahabala, I have never felt for another. His anxious face, with that dark mole on his left cheek, would appear vividly before my eyes each day, making me yearn for his friendship. Yet, whenever I drew near, he would find some excuse and slip away. One day, he suddenly vanished; he stopped coming to class. I searched, wandering through the streets of Kashi. I was distraught, fearing someone might have harmed him.

One day, I found him sitting on the verandah of a house. I stared in surprise—he sat alone, lost in thought, fidgeting with his beads. Unable to restrain myself, I ran to him, took his hand and pulled him up. He lifted his heavy eyes and said, “Pranesh, go your own way.” I held him, shook him. He rose in anger and said, “Do you want the truth? Listen. I have abandoned my studies. Do you know what I live for now? Come inside. I will show you.” And pulling me in, he led me inside.
Samskara 103

They showed a girl, lying asleep in the afternoon on a thin mattress. She lay with her arms outstretched. From the allure of her attire alone, it was clear she was a courtesan. I trembled, seized by fear and wonder. Mahabala said, “You understand now, Pranesh. Do not think of me any longer. Go.”

I walked away, as if in a daze, seeing nothing, my mind turned to stone once more. I had stubbornly resolved to steer my life in the opposite direction from Mahabala, who had fallen into corruption. Yet, whenever I saw Narayanappa here, I was reminded of Mahabala. Though there was a vast gulf between the two.

Now I feel: I must see Mahabala. I must ask him: Why did you so abruptly change the course of your life? What experience, what desire, what enchantment led you thus? What would you tell me to do now? Did you find complete satisfaction in the pleasures of women? Could a life as prosperous as yours be fulfilled by a single woman? Ah, it shines forth now.

Praneshacharya rose and began to walk. The root lies there. The disappointment I received from Mahabala must have remained within me. Unconsciously, I must have seen Mahabala in Narayanappa. To find solace for my defeat there, I must have tried to conquer Narayanappa. But I failed, I failed—fell, utterly defeated. I have become what I fought against. Why? Why? Where, how, did I fail?

If I try to search, everything gets entangled in knots. Wherever I look, one knot is tied to another. From Mahabala to Narayanappa, from Narayanappa to my own stubbornness, to the Puranas I studied, their consequences, and finally, the desire that arose in me for the silver breasts, the form I now possess, all of it was being prepared throughout my life—indirectly. The moment when Chandri joined me, thus—
Samskara

When I look back, it always seems as if it arrived unexpectedly, unbidden. There must have been a moment when everything within me surged out—like rats bursting forth from a granary. Then, the memory of the agrahara returns, bringing with it an unbearable sense of revulsion. The agrahara stands before me now as the clear embodiment of the dilemma I face—my entire life demands an explanation, and the only thing clear to me is that I must flee from it. Perhaps I should go to Chandri, become like Mahabala. Yes—let it take a definite shape. Let me escape this Trishanku state. I must walk away now, unseen by any eye, unnoticed by anyone.

As he walked, Praneshacharya began to feel as though someone was following him through the forest. He felt as if a pair of eyes were fixed steadily upon him. He straightened his back and continued walking. He felt the urge to turn and look behind him. He grew anxious, uneasy, and finally turned around. In the distance, he saw a young man, grown to adulthood, hurrying toward him with quick steps. Praneshacharya too quickened his pace. When he glanced back again, the young man was still walking rapidly, matching his speed. He continued at the same pace, but the other did not seem to falter. Being young, the stranger walked even faster and began to draw closer. Praneshacharya grew anxious, wondering if this might be someone he knew. However fast he walked, the young man drew nearer. Praneshacharya’s legs began to ache, and his pace slowed. The young man caught up with him, and, breathing heavily, began to walk alongside him. Praneshacharya looked at him, wondering who he might be. The face was unfamiliar—
“I am Putta, from the Malera caste. I’m on my way to the chariot festival at the fair. Are you headed that way too?”
He began, introducing himself. Praneshacharya did not feel like speaking. Without knowing what to say, he looked at the young man’s face.

They looked at me. On his dark, withered face, beads of sweat had gathered. Because of his long, prominent nose, his face bore the look of a stubborn man. His eyes, set close together, gave his gaze a sharpness that made anyone caught in it feel uneasy. Except for the sacred thread, he wore only a shirt and a dhoti, appearing like a young man from the town.
“I saw you from behind, and from your gait I thought you must be someone familiar. Now that I see your face, it feels as though I’ve seen you somewhere before…”
Though it was just the customary way villagers began a conversation, Praneshacharya felt irritated.
“No, I’m from below the Ghats. I’m out on some business,” Praneshacharya tried to end the conversation.
“Oh, I know people from below the Ghats too. My uncle’s house is there. I go there now and then. Where exactly is your village below the Ghats?”
“Kundapura.”
“Oh, Kundapura? Do you know Sheenappayya there?”
“No,” Praneshacharya replied curtly, and started walking again.
But Putta, who had come seeking conversation, did not seem satisfied with so little.
“That Sheenappayya is very important to us. He and my uncle’s family are very close. My wife’s younger sister is married to his second son…”

“Hm, hm,” muttered Praneshacharya as he walked on. But this was not something that could be shaken off so easily, even if he tried to leave it behind. Deciding that if the fellow was in a hurry, he could go ahead, Praneshacharya, feeling weary, sat down at the foot of a tree. Putta seemed pleased by this. He too…
Samskara:

Ushyappa sat down, pulled a matchbox from his shirt pocket, and offered a beedi. Praneshacharya declined. Ushyappa lit the beedi for himself. Praneshacharya, pretending that this brief rest had restored his strength, rose and set off again. Putta too stood up and followed. “If you meet someone to talk to on the road, you don’t even realize how the distance passes, do you? For me, I just need someone to talk to, that’s all, Appa,” Putta said, walking beside Praneshacharya with a bright, curious smile.

Meanwhile, after performing his wife’s funeral rites, Praneshacharya set out, intending to walk as far as his legs would carry him. Within a couple of hours, word of all that had happened reached everyone in Parijatapura—the news that some outcaste had cremated Narayanappa’s corpse. The only ones who kept silent were the young men of Parijatapura who, emboldened for a fleeting moment by drink, had resolved to perform Narayanappa’s samskara, but then, overcome by fear or weakness, had fled. Unable to confess the truth of what they had witnessed, they sealed their lips.

Most troubled of all was the moneylender, Manjayya. What had happened was a string of deaths, one after another: first Narayanappa, then Dasacharya, then Praneshacharya’s wife—there could be only one meaning: this was a curse. Manjayya, who was well-versed in the affairs of Shimoga’s mandi-pet, courts, and offices, laughed at the other Brahmins’ anxieties. Everyone believed that all this was happening because of Narayanappa’s untimely death and the failure to perform his samskara, a breach of duty. Manjayya, though he felt a pang—“Ayyoh, only the other day Dasacharya ate uppittu at my house, and now he’s dead”—even so, he consoled himself, thinking, “At least I didn’t let that Brahmin inside my home.”

Fear. That day, when all the Brahmins of Durvasapura gathered and announced that Narayanappa, who had come from Shimoga, had suddenly developed a fever and died, suspicion had already arisen among them. Yet, they hesitated even to utter the dreadful name of that disease aloud. Why should I be so forward, I thought. And now, rats are dropping dead, we are on the verge of fleeing the agrahara, like refugees at the border. After hearing the news that the authorities had come because of the rats, all doubt vanished completely. For sixteen annas to the rupee, she was certain of her guess. Besides, the 'Tayinadu' newspaper that arrived yesterday—even if it was last week's issue—had printed the news in a corner: “Plague in Shimoga.” Narayanappa brought the plague. It is a scourge that spreads like wildfire. All these days we remained silent, bound by some blind faith, leaving the corpse of the one who died without performing his samskara—like carrying a millstone on our own heads. We are fools. I too have become a simpleton!

“Quickly, harness the cart!” shouted those standing in the chavadis. There was not a moment to lose. In one way or another, the plague would cross the river and reach their agrahara. If a single rat that died of plague were to be carried by a kite or a crow and dropped in their agrahara, that would be enough—everything would be over. Standing outside the house, he shouted loudly so that all could hear: No one should go near Durvasapura until I return from the town.

But, being the leader of the agrahara, he could not bring himself to instill in anyone the fear that this might be plague. Without delay, he had the cart harnessed, settled himself against the cushion in the bullock cart, and told the driver to rush to Tirthahalli. In his shrewd, practical mind, a clear plan had formed: First—inform the municipal authorities and have the corpse removed. Second—bring a doctor and have inoculations done. Third—bring a pump and fumigate the air.
Samskara
...must be filled into all the holes of the anthills, and the rat burrows must be closed.

Fourth—if necessary, the entire agrahara must be abandoned by everyone—for a little while at least. Along the way, chanting “untouchable, untouchable,” they encouraged the cart driver, who, turning the tails of the oxen, urged them onward. The cart sped down the road toward Tirthahalli.

Having left the matha in despair, Garudacharya, Lakshmanacharya, and the other Brahmins came to the agrahara where Padmanabhacharya, stricken with fever, lay bedridden. On arriving, they saw that Padmanabhacharya had lost consciousness. One of the agrahara’s Brahmins, in haste to inform Padmanabhacharya’s wife of the situation, had run to her house. Another young man had gone to the town to fetch a doctor. This filled Garudacharya with dread. In the matha, Gundacharya was lying ill with fever; in Kaimara, Dasacharya was bedridden; and here, Padmanabhacharya’s tongue had fallen limp—there was no doubt that some calamity had befallen the agrahara.

Lakshmanacharya confronted Garudacharya, who had opposed Narayanappa’s funeral rites. But everyone insisted this was not the time for blame; they urged him to quickly go and complete the samskara, and then offer penance to the deity for any transgression. With a reluctant heart, they left Padmanabhacharya behind and set out. But before leaving, Garudacharya folded his hands to the people of the agrahara and pleaded, “Please, when the doctor arrives, take him to the matha and have him give the same medicine to Gundacharya.”

No one had the courage to speak a word along the way. A heavy gloom had descended. In his heart, Garudacharya prayed, “I will offer penance to Maruti, forgive us.” Thus, burdened with heavy hearts, they walked and walked, and finally reached Kaimara.
Samskara 109

What did they see—what was there to see? The ashes of Dasacharya, the news of Praneshacharya’s wife’s passing. This threw all the Brahmins into confusion. The world as they had known it was thrown into disarray. It was as if they had glimpsed a ghost in the darkness. Like children, they sat huddled against the wall, eyes brimming with tears. The elder, Subbannacharya, spoke words of consolation, urged them to be brave.
After sitting in silence for a long time, Garudacharya asked in a faint voice, “Are there still rats falling in our agrahara?”
Subbannacharya replied, “What do you mean?”
“Nothing. The vulture is perched on the house,” said Garudacharya.
“Once the samskara is performed, all will be auspicious,” Subbannacharya said.
“I will not go to the agrahara,” Garudacharya replied.
The other Brahmins muttered among themselves: “How can we perform the samskara for that rotting corpse? Even four cartloads of firewood will not suffice to burn it.”
Lakshmanacharya said, “Get up.”
Garudacharya said, “I am exhausted—let someone else do it.”
“If you, who are learned in ritual, sit here paralyzed by fear, what will become of the rest?” Subbannacharya said.
“I cannot,” Garudacharya replied.
“Get up, get up,” urged Lakshmanacharya. “There is no one left in the agrahara. What will happen to the cattle? There is no one to tie them in the shed, no one to milk them,” he pleaded.
“Yes, yes, yes,” the other Brahmins agreed.
Chanting “Hari Hari,” they set out. All along the way, they walked reciting the Raghavendra Stotra.

Though they had vowed to offer a chicken to Panjurli and a sheep at the next new moon, Belli’s father and mother both died on the very night Praneshacharya’s wife passed away. Hearing Belli’s wails, all the neighboring Holayas gathered. In the darkness...
Samskara

The black, naked bodies sat dumbfounded around the temple for half an hour. Then, the pyre at the Sogeya shrine was set alight. In an instant, the flames leapt up, licking at the women who tended the fire. The silver—who had stood there in fear—forgot all decorum, abandoned her veil, and, like a mouse, darted away into the darkness.

The little Malera boy had begun to follow him like a shadow of fate. If he stopped, the boy stopped; if he sat, the boy sat; if he walked fast, the boy hurried; if he slowed, the boy slowed—he would not leave his side. Praneshacharya found it increasingly vexing. At a time when he wished to sit with closed eyes and contemplate his own fate, this little fellow kept chattering away. Even though Praneshacharya gave him no encouragement, the boy was desperate for his company. Not knowing that he was Vedantashiroamani Praneshacharya, the boy behaved with him as he would with any ordinary Brahmin, as if he were speaking to a poor, wandering priest.

His reason told him that it was not proper to walk so far without sandals. The boy insisted that in Tirthahalli, a pair could be had for three rupees. He lectured on whether comfort or money was more important. He showed off his own sandals—“See, I’ve had these for a year, and they haven’t worn out!” he declared. “I want to talk,” he said. “Come, give me a riddle to solve,” he pleaded.

Suppressing the irritation that rose within him, Praneshacharya fell silent. Then, he posed a riddle: “There is a river, a boat, and a man. With him, he has a bundle of grass, a tiger, and a cow. He must ferry them across the river, one by one. You must see that the cow does not eat the grass, and the tiger does not eat the cow. In this way, all three must be taken from this bank to the other. Let’s see how sharp your mind is,” he said, and, with supreme satisfaction, lit a beedi.

He had been irritated. Yet, despite his anger, Praneshacharya found his mind troubled by the riddle. “Did it shine or not? Did it shine or not?” Puttana kept pestering him as they walked. Praneshacharya knew the answer, but was reluctant to speak. If he solved the riddle, it would be as if he extended a hand of friendship to Puttana. If he did not, Puttana would think him a fool. Now, he was caught in a dilemma, unable to decide what to do. He thought, “Let me appear a fool, a simpleton, in his eyes.”

“Did it shine?” Puttana asked again, puffing on his beedi, not really wanting to talk. Praneshacharya shook his head as if to say no. “Ho ho ho!” Puttana burst out laughing, almost stumbling, and gave away the answer to the riddle. This made his contempt for the learned Brahmin grow even more. “Another riddle!” he said.
“No,” Praneshacharya replied.
“All right, then you ask me one. Defeat me, come on!” Puttana challenged.
“I don’t know any,” said Praneshacharya.
“Poor thing,” Puttana thought.

Not knowing what else to say, Puttana bit his tongue. “Acharya, did you know? That Shyama, who used to dress up in colors at the Kundapura fair—he’s passed away, his sins are all washed away,” he began, introducing a new topic.
“Ah, poor fellow. I didn’t know,” Praneshacharya said.
“Then you must have been away from the village for a long time,” said Puttana.
Praneshacharya was relieved to see a fork in the road ahead.
“Which way are you headed?” he asked, stopping to question Puttana.
“This way,” Puttana pointed down one path.
“I’m going this way,” Praneshacharya said, pointing to another footpath.
“Both roads lead to the fair, just a little detour—that’s all. I’m not in any hurry… I’ll come along with you,” Puttana declared.
He took some jaggery from his bag, offered it to Praneshacharya, and began to eat some himself. Praneshacharya, hungry, accepted Puttana’s jaggery.
Samskara
...felt grateful about it. Wherever he went, whatever he did, human company seemed to cling to him like fate.

As he chewed a small piece of jaggery, he began to speak more intimately. “You must be married, aren’t you? Or is it not so? Forgive me, I’m asking like a fool. How many children do you have? Or none at all? Ah, that’s a pity. I have two children. Both boys. I told you, didn’t I, that my wife was brought from Kundapura? There’s something—whether to laugh or to cry, I do not know. For her, her parents are everything. If she misses visiting them one month, she insists on going the next. Tell me, who can afford to send anyone in these times, with the bus fare being two rupees? And she won’t listen if I say no. Even after two children, she hasn’t gained any sense. She’s very young, you see, and not old enough, perhaps. My mother-in-law is a bit of a sharp-tongued woman, but my father-in-law is wise. He knows how to handle things, whatever they are. My mother-in-law once said—‘What right does a son-in-law have to scold my daughter?’ But never once has such a word come from my father-in-law’s mouth. Even if I scold her, she doesn’t learn. If I don’t send her to her parents, she threatens to jump into the well. I don’t know what to do. Except for this one bad habit, she’s good in every other way. She cooks, she washes dishes, she keeps everything in order—except for this one thing. What do you say to that...?”
Praneshacharya smiled without replying. Puttana too laughed.
“To know a woman’s mind, and to trace the path of a fish in water—both are impossible, isn’t that what the elders say?” he said.
“True, true,” replied Praneshacharya.
At that, Puttana’s words came to a pause. The Acharya felt as if he must be searching for his wife’s mind in some world beyond words. Now, this was his own riddle. This, I must first...
Samskara

I did not look at it thoroughly. At the moment of decision in my life— with Naranappa, with Mahabala, with my wife, with the other Brahmins of the agrahara, with the very dharma I lived by—every relationship, everything that defined me, was to be decided in that impartial darkness of the forest that arose unexpectedly. Suddenly, I turned away. The consequences were not mine alone; they became profound for the agrahara as well. That is, the question of my resolve was not merely my own—it became a question that encompassed my entire agrahara. This is the root of the confusion, the anxiety, the moral crisis.

When the question of Naranappa’s funeral rites arose, I did not try to resolve it from my personal perspective. I bound myself to the dharmashastra, to God. Isn’t this why we created the dharmashastra? Because our personal decisions are so deeply intertwined with society? For— in every one of our actions, we involve our ancestors, our gurus, the divine, the human family. That is why there is a moral crisis. But when I lay with Chandri, did I experience such a crisis? Was that a decision measured, weighed, and made? Now it has all become hazy, indistinct. That decision, or that act, tore me away from my earthly world, from the world of Brahmins, from my wife’s life, from my beliefs. As a result, now I am fluttering like a thread in the wind.
Release from this? Release?
“Acharya,” said Putta.
“What is it?”
“Should we wait any longer?”
“Give it,” said Praneshacharya. Putta handed him the betel leaf. “Otherwise, isn’t it easy to lose the way? For the mind—”
Samskara
“If you’re bored, I’ll give you another riddle to solve. ‘It plays, it runs, it stands still and watches’—tell me, what is it?” he said, lighting another beedi.

So, perhaps the root of all my anxiety lies in the dream—my having slept with Chandri in my dream. The result: this present Trishanku state. Only by performing an act deliberately, consciously, with full awareness and resolve, can I be released from this. Now, I am like a thread in the wind, a cloud shaped by the air that blows it. I have become a mere thing; only through a definite act do I become a human being again. I become responsible for my own life. That is… that is… instead of wavering at the crossroads, I will take the bus to Kundapura and stay with Chandri. Thus, I will put an end to all my torment. In full consciousness, I will recreate myself…
“Did you get it?” asked Putta, with a small smile.
“The one that plays is a monkey, the one that runs is water, the one that stands still and watches is a stone,” said Praneshacharya.

“Bravo! Well done. Do you know what they call me in my village? Ogatana Putta—the Riddler Putta. I’ve got a whole load of riddles. If you walk a hundred miles with me, I’ll give you a riddle for every mile,” said Putta, flicking away his beedi.

After walking in the sun, Garuda, Lakshmana, and the other Brahmins reached Durvasapura as the heat of the day was waning. They felt some relief when, upon entering the agrahara, they saw there were no boundary marks on the houses. Lakshmanacharya said softly, “I’ll go and see what’s become of the cattle at home. You go ahead…”

When Garudacharya snapped, “First the rites of samskara, then your household chores,” Lakshmanacharya did not have the courage to protest. All of them gathered and went to Praneshacharya’s house. Each felt they must offer some solace for his sorrow. But when they called, there was no answer from within. If one entered the house, it was as if a rat had died inside. Because of this, no one dared to step into their own homes either. As soon as they reached the agrahara street, a heavy silence fell. The agrahara itself seemed to be crumbling into ruin. “What are we to do now?” they all wondered together.

“Shava samskara,” said one Brahmin. But none had the courage to enter Narayanappa’s house and behold the corpse, which by now might be decomposed and grotesque. Garudacharya devised a plan: “Praneshacharya must have gone to the river or somewhere else. Let us wait until he returns.”
Lakshmanacharya said, “There is no time to lose. At least let us begin the preparations for the funeral rites.”
“To the shed,” said one Brahmin.
“We must cut down the mango tree,” said another.
“How can we burn a decomposed corpse in the green wood shed?” asked a third.
“It will suffice to burn him with the firewood from his own house,” said Lakshmanacharya.
“You didn’t offer your own firewood, did you?” Garuda taunted him.

But when they circled Narayanappa’s house and looked in the backyard, there was not enough firewood. They called out, “Chandri! Chandri!” but there was no reply. “She must have run off to Kundapura, that woman who ruined the town,” the Brahmins muttered.

“What else can we do? Let each house bring a bundle of firewood and leave it at the cremation ground,” said Garudacharya. All agreed, and from each backyard they carried a headload of firewood, and took it to the cremation ground two miles away.
When they returned to the agrahara, Praneshacharya was still not there.
“The corpse,” said one Brahmin.
“Let Praneshacharya return,” said Garuda.
“Very well,” said Lakshmanacharya.
A sense of dread gripped them all—to go inside...
Samskara

Garuda said, “It is not right to proceed without informing Praneshacharya.” The Brahmins replied, “Let us make all the preparations and wait.” So they lit a fire in a pot in front of Narayanappa’s house, brought the ritual dolls, and sat forming a circle—waiting for Praneshacharya.

By around three in the afternoon, Praneshacharya and Putta reached the Melige lake. Walking along the cart-track, their bodies were covered in red dust. As they stepped into the lake to wash their hands and feet, Putta said, “We’ve talked so much, but I haven’t told you anything about myself, have I?” While washing his face, Acharya was seized by a fear: what if someone he knew from Melige recognized him here? Again, fear had taken root—he was annoyed at himself. One consolation: all the Brahmins of Melige were Smarthas, so they were strangers. And in the bustle of the fair, who would notice him? But no matter how much he tried to reassure himself, the fear remained. Surely, someone he knew would have come for the fair. But so what? Once he had made up his mind, what was there to fear? Yet the fear persisted. Why this fear, if it was for no reason? He must find its root. He must tear out this fear, root and all. How boldly Narayanappa had lived with Chandri in the midst of the agrahara, unashamed! If I were to join Chandri, would I hide my face in shame? What a life, he thought with disgust.

Putta, wiping his face, said, “Perhaps you’re wondering why I’m telling you all this? You might think, ‘What’s with this fellow, he won’t stop talking.’ But listen—I’ll tell you. Though you aren’t much of a talker, you need people, you need conversation. You have a gentle nature. Poor people.”
Samskara 103.

He said, “Just say yes or no, and I’ll tell you what kind of people they are just by looking at their faces. Why hide anything from you? Do you think I don’t know what sort of people you are? Haven’t you always thought of me as a Malera? If you want, I’ll tell you more. My father was a noble Brahmin. He cared for my mother, whom he kept, even better than his wife. He even performed my sacred thread ceremony. If you want to see—” he said, pulling his janivara from under his shirt to show them. “That’s why all my friends are Brahmins. Come, let’s go,” he said, climbing up the bund of the tank. “It’s fitting, then, that I mingle with people and do what I do. One of my names is Ogatina Putta; the other is Harate Putta. In short, I need people,” he laughed.

In the bustle of the festival, the chariot had already been drawn to the field. The peak of the chariot, adorned with images of Kanya, Vrishchika, Mithuna, and others, stood resplendent in the middle of the village. Two thick ropes were tied along the road to the chariot. The devotees had pulled the ratha halfway from the shed, leaving fruits and coconuts as offerings. A priest sat inside the chariot, having climbed the ladder, and a young Brahmin climbed up and down, handing over the offerings the devotees brought. Around the chariot, a large crowd waited, holding their fruits and coconuts. Praneshacharya anxiously searched the crowd for anyone he knew. In the midst of the dense throng, where even a sesame seed would not fall to the ground, Putta took Acharya’s hand and led him to a shop, where they bought coconuts and fruits. When the crowd thinned, they managed to perform the puja. “Now let’s wander a bit, Acharya,” Putta said.

As they stepped out of the crowd, the sound of pipes filled the air; in every village boy’s mouth was a pipe bought with coins begged from their parents, each making its own peculiar noise. The scent of camphor and incense drifted everywhere.

The scent of new clothes. The song of the balloon seller. In one corner, a Bombay box—if you give him a coin, he strikes the anklet-adorned box with a stick, dancing as he displays it: “See the city of Delhi, see the office of the Collector, see the market of Bangalore, see the palace of the Mysore Maharaja, ah, witness the splendor of the durbar, see the Lord of Tirupati, ah! See the courtesan of Bombay, ah, the courtesan of Bombay!” The jingling dance comes to a halt. “Bombay box—box—just a coin, a coin!” he shouts.

Puttana could not simply walk past and ignore it. “Acharyare, I want to see,” he said. “Very well,” said Praneshacharya, “but don’t go up the hill. Sit here.” Puttana pulled the black curtain over his face and sat, watching through the peephole. Now, should I leave him here and go on alone? Acharya wondered, and then felt a pang of guilt. But if I keep him with me, there will be no peace; I must be alone now—so he walked on.

He had not gone far when he heard, “Achare!” Turning back, he saw Puttana. “I thought you had left me behind. But the Bombay box man showed me the way you went—go ahead,” he said. Praneshacharya felt a strange sensation run through him. He wanted to scold the boy. But how could he hurt a creature who, without asking, without expecting, had offered him a hand of friendship? Let him experience it, he thought.

“Ah, look!” said Puttana. The dombe’s performance was going on. A beautiful woman, her body as supple as a serpent, stretched out her arms and legs, balancing perfectly as she lay swinging on a bamboo pole, her bare stomach exposed. The dombe beat his drum. In another moment, the graceful woman swung down from the pole and began to dance. The crowd threw coins. Puttana too tossed a coin.
As they neared the temple, on either side were people with stumps for hands, stumps for legs, the blind, those with nothing but a hole where their nose should be…
Samskara 119

The two men with deformities, each with their own kind of disability, crawled on the ground, begging. The most strikingly deformed among them was tossing shells, and Putta walked over to him. Ahead, at a shop where women had just unloaded their colorful ribbons, he bought a yard of tape for his wife. “She desires this,” he thought. He bought two tin whistles of different colors for the children and blew into them to test. “They’ll like this,” he thought.

In the midst of the bustle and celebration, Praneshacharya felt himself adrift, like a restless spirit, an uneasy presence among the crowd. Putta spotted a soda shop. “Come, let’s have a Crush,” he said. “No, I don’t drink such things,” replied Praneshacharya. At a Konkani man’s soda stall, Putta pointed out a bottle filled with bright red liquid and said, “One Crush.” The shop was filled with shy women, Gowdas, and children, all sipping the fragrant, fizzy soda Crush. Hair oiled and neatly combed, adorned with a round flower, new sarees draped, the Gowdas in fresh shirts. The sound of the marble being popped from the bottle’s neck—“kunk,” “goyik”—and the sharp, sweet gas escaping with a “garak” after drinking—these were moments of anticipation, experience, and satisfaction. Among the many joys the fair offered, this was one. Everyone had already set aside the necessary coins for it, expecting this pleasure.

Standing apart from this world of simple joys, Praneshacharya looked at the gathered people. Putta’s face lit up after the “garak” of the soda. “Come, let’s go,” he said. “You didn’t take anything for yourself, did you?” he asked.

Thus, amid the noise, the excitement, the balloons, whistles, sweets, the sound of Crush bottles, the temple bells, the splendor of the women’s bangle stalls, Praneshacharya wandered after Putta, as if in a daze.

They walked on. Everywhere, there were eyes full of intent, except for his own, which could not be intent on anything. Putt is all right. My meeting with him too must be fate. To fulfill the resolve I have made, I must have the worthiness to become as intent in life as Putt. This is Chandri’s world. I belong neither here nor there. I am caught in duality. The aroma of coffee and masala dosa drifted by. Putt stopped, and so did the Acharya.
“Come, have a little coffee,” said Putt.
“I don’t want any,” said Praneshacharya.
“This is a Brahmin hotel. It’s come from Tirthahalli just for the festival. There’s no fault in it. Inside, there’s a separate place for madi-Brahmins.”
“No. I don’t want coffee.”

“That won’t do. The coffee I offer you, you must drink. Come,” said Putt, taking his hand and leading him inside. Praneshacharya sat on the mat unwillingly, glancing around in fear, wondering if someone he knew might be there. If a Vedanta Shiromani were to be seen drinking hotel coffee… He cursed himself, wishing first to be free of this fear.

Putt went and sat a little distance away, showing respect for Praneshacharya’s Brahminhood. “Two special coffees,” he said to the boy standing in front. He paid two annas, and as he sipped the coffee brought in a tumbler, he said, “Useless festival coffee.” Praneshacharya, thirsty, drank the coffee and felt at peace. He felt a surge of energy. They stepped outside.

“If you wish, you can go eat at the temple. Today, until six o’clock, there’s food served for Brahmins,” said Putt. Having not eaten for so many days, Praneshacharya suddenly longed for a hot meal of rice and sambar. But at once, he—
Samskara 121

Isn’t this a time of impurity? One must not eat in the temple. There was a belief that if the ritual was not performed, the chariot would not move forward. But didn’t Narayanappa seize Ganapati’s honor and prevail? He felt he did not possess the courage to so completely reject Brahminhood and walk away from it. Then what value did his resolve to live with Chandri hold, he wondered bitterly. A resolve must be complete. If you tie yourself, tie yourself fully. If you let go, let go completely. That is the path beyond duality. That is the path to escape fear. How decisively Mahabala had resolved...

“Wait a moment, Acharyare, look there,” said Putta. In the distance, on a mound, there was a group of Shudras who seemed entranced. “Come, let’s go see. There must be a cockfight,” said Putta. Praneshacharya’s heart thudded. Yet he walked with Putta—bowing to fate, he stood a little apart from the group and watched. The smell of toddy made him nauseous. Two roosters, their legs bound, were flapping their wings—‘rap, rap’—pecking each other with their beaks, leaping at one another, as the people sat crouched on their haunches—on tiptoe, mouths agape, encircling the birds. Such intense, sharp, fierce gazes—Praneshacharya had never seen in his life. The five vital airs themselves seemed to be in the eyes of those watching—life itself, and the two roosters. No, four wings, four legs. Cluck, cluck, cluck, cluck—all around, forty eyes. The shining beaks of the red-crested roosters. Sunlight glinting, dazzling, sparkling. Ah, what a marvel! They struck, they struck, they leapt and sat. Praneshacharya felt dizzy. It was as if he had suddenly entered a world of demons. In the depths of the underworld, in some cave of darkness, the eyes of these entranced creatures—
Samskara:

If harsh single-mindedness is one aspect, then, as a Brahmin, he sat there mortally afraid that he might wither and decay away. The sound of the two cock owners goading their birds into a frenzy did not seem to come from a human throat. He became certain that he had no capacity whatsoever to survive in this world of such cruel, sharp emotions. If one side of desire is tenderness, on the other must lurk this demonic cunning. The shame he had felt the day Narayanappa had spurned him and walked away—when his own sense of self had seemed to splinter—returned to him, raw and fresh.

The two cocks, battered and bloodied, were forcibly separated, their wounds tended, and then set to fight again. Meanwhile, a small, unfamiliar boy had struck up a wager with another onlooker. “This cock is mine,” said the boy. “If it wins, I get two annas,” said the stranger. “If mine wins, I get four,” said the boy. “Eight,” said the other. “Ten,” said the boy. “Twelve,” said the other. “Let’s see,” said the boy.

Praneshacharya watched anxiously. What would become of this impetuous boy if he lost all the money he had? But to his great surprise, the boy won. Yet, as soon as he stood up to leave, the loser demanded, “One more round.” “No,” said the boy. The man, drunk, lunged at the boy to strike him. Praneshacharya intervened. Seeing a Brahmin, the man swallowed his anger. As the crowd began to press in, asking, “What’s happening? What’s happening?” Praneshacharya pulled the boy away and walked off.

The boy, puffed up with pride at winning twelve annas, did not seem at all diminished by the experience. But Praneshacharya, all at once, felt a surge of affection for him. If only I had a son, I could have advised him with love, he thought.
“Yes, Puttanna, let us take the road now,” said Praneshacharya, trying to end their brief friendship then and there.
"Samskara 123"
"Which direction are you traveling?" asked Putta, his small face tightening with curiosity. Acharya wondered what this boy expected from him, why he seemed so intent.
"Well, I haven’t decided yet," he replied.
"If you’re going that far, at least have your meal at the temple before you leave," Putta insisted, almost pleading.
To avoid further embarrassment, Praneshacharya said, "I have to see a goldsmith."
"Why?" Putta pressed, unmoved.
"I need to sell a gold ring."
"Why? If you’re short of money for expenses, take these twelve annas from me for now. You can return it another time."
Praneshacharya felt utterly at a loss as to how to escape from such a man. Putta’s concern clung to him like a creeper winding around one’s feet.
"No, Putta, I need more than just a little money. I have to catch a bus to Kundapura. There are some other expenses as well," Praneshacharya said, unable to shake off Putta’s persistence.
"Oh, is that so? Come then, I know a goldsmith here. What do you want to sell?"
"The sacred ring worn for the yajñopavīta," Praneshacharya admitted, unable to hide it any longer.

"Let me see it," said Putta, extending his hand. Embarrassed in the crowd, Praneshacharya took off the yajñopavīta ring and handed it over. Putta examined it in his palm and said, "Don’t accept anything less than fifteen rupees for this."
The two of them entered a lane and went to the goldsmith’s house. In front of a wooden chest, the goldsmith sat polishing a ring, his silver-rimmed spectacles perched straight on his nose.
Samskara.

“What is it?” he asked, seeing Putta, who replied, “Well, Puttaiah’s ring has come to us,” and offered it. The goldsmith weighed it on his little scale, rubbed it on the touchstone, and said, “Ten rupees.” Putta retorted, “If it’s less than fifteen, there’s nothing to discuss.” The bargaining talk made Acharya uncomfortable. “The price of gold has fallen,” said the goldsmith. “That’s none of my concern. Will you give fifteen or not?” Putta looked at Acharya, raising his eyebrows as if to display his business acumen. Acharya replied, “If it’s ten, let it be ten. That’s enough for my expenses now,” unwilling to prolong the discussion. Putta was annoyed. The goldsmith’s face broadened with satisfaction. He counted out ten rupees, and the transaction was done. Praneshacharya said, “Thank you,” and stepped outside.

No sooner had they stepped out than Putta began to grumble—like a wife who feels her husband has been cheated: “If I were to do you a favor, my own honor would be lost, you know. My word has no value with him anymore—let it be—but five rupees is not a small name for us! In this Kali Yuga, you mustn’t be so naïve, understand? Have you heard, even goldsmiths steal their own brother’s gold?”
“I was in need of money. I acted rashly. Forgive me,” Praneshacharya said humbly, not wishing to hurt Putta’s feelings. Putta softened:

“The moment I saw you, I knew it. You’re a very gentle soul. You shouldn’t be sent anywhere alone. I’ll put you on the bus myself and then go back. Now, do as I say. Our village folks are here. I need to meet them. Come along. Then we’ll go to the temple and have a meal. Don’t worry. Until evening, there will be row after row for the feast.”
Samskara 125:

Food. Then, at night, sleep somewhere here, and in the morning, walk five miles to Tirthahalli. From there, there’s a bus to Agumbe. If you take a taxi down the ghat, there’s a direct bus to Kundapura,” he said.
For the expenses on the way to Kundapura, the Acharya tied the money, gotten from selling his ring, tightly around his waist. “Be careful with the money,” Putta reminded him gently.

As he went to eat, Acharya thought, perhaps he had let himself slip, just a little, with this man. Seeing Putta, who had entered his life without any expectation, he felt this must surely be a situation born of prarabdha karma. Perhaps it was the repayment of some debt from a previous birth, being settled in this way. There is no escape from the company of other humans. Like a creeper used for support by the foot. With what face can I ever say, “My life is my own”?

“Come this way,” Putta said, leading him through a narrow lane along the crowded temple path. Walking on, they came to a deserted place. There was a stream there. To cross it, a bamboo pole served as a bridge. They climbed over a fence and entered a field.

As they walked along the edge of the field, Praneshacharya remembered the cockfight pit. How one rooster would mount another, wings flailing, and plunge its beak into the flesh—tearing, pecking, deeper and deeper. The knife glinting sharply in the sun. And those eyes. Even when the scent of blood was washed away and the body lay limp, the wounded bird would still twitch and peck, kok kok, as if unwilling to die.

The demon world of stubborn desire. There, I was like a captive ghoul. A sudden fear: by the act of my own decision, have I become part of that world? And then, that dombera girl. She appeared vividly before him, dressed in tight clothes, practicing her acrobatics at the tip of the bamboo, brushing the sky. She let go of the rope. She leapt. If pushed, she would spin and tumble like a marble. Colored water, the sharpness of toddy—
Samskara

Expectation, experience, satisfaction. Eyes intent, absorbed. Eyes, amidst the colored tape and balloons, around the chariot’s spire, behind my back, on both sides. Eyes around wings, bangles, beaks, claws. Of the same form, intent. The non-duality of desires and satisfactions. Tat tvam asi. Tat tvam asi. I am unsettled: the unease of losing ghostliness and attaining demonhood.
“Do you know where we are going now?” Putta, lighting a small beedi, asked with a mischievous smile.
Praneshacharya shook his head to say he did not know.

“If you don’t mind, Marayare, I have agreed. If someone says, ‘Walk without asking where or why,’ you just walk. I am a bit like that too, Marayare. Once, just like this, I went all the way to Shimoga with a friend. My uncles were so displeased—‘Putta? If you let our Putta go, you’ll never get him back; if you get him back, you’ll never let him go,’ they would say.”
“You said we’re going to your Paiki’s house, didn’t you?”
“Acharya, address me in the singular. You calling me in the plural is not good for my lifespan.”
“So be it.”

“There’s a garden right here. Look, that one. A woman from our Paiki’s family has taken it on lease. She lives alone. A very courageous woman. One must wash hands before touching her, such is her form. She’s a distant relative of mine. She has great respect for Vedic Brahmins like you. She’ll just show her face and let us go. Otherwise, she’ll say, ‘Oh Putta, you came, did you? You just show your face and rush off as if you’re in a hurry to live or die.’ Look, I don’t like hurting anyone’s feelings. A human life—who knows if it’s now or in the next moment? Why should we hurt anyone, tell me? That’s why I say yes to everything—
Samskara . 127

I will let go. But listen, Marayare, my wife alone keeps pestering me every month to take her to the temple fair. At first, I said yes. Then I said no. I even tried beating her. But then I feel sorry—perhaps you have heard the song: "He beat his wife! But inside, he was shaken! He went in and held her feet! He went in, held her feet, and pleaded! 'Am I not yours, your servant?'"—that is how I am.

“We have arrived,” said Putta, who was sitting on the bench above the garden, and they entered the house. “Is she here or not? She might have gone to the fair as an excuse,” said Putta, calling out, “Padmavati!” From the mat on the veranda, where Praneshacharya sat, a woman’s gentle voice replied, “I am here.” A voice full of warmth. And fear. Who is she? Why has Putta brought me here?

“Come in,” invited the same voice. Praneshacharya turned, startled. She stood holding the pillar, her hand raised above the threshold. The moment his eyes met hers, something fluttered in his chest. “See whom I have brought. Acharya,” said Putta. “Come in,” she repeated, shyly. “Shall I bring you some Ganga water?” she asked. “At least have some milk or fruit,” she insisted, and went inside.

Praneshacharya broke into a sweat. There was no doubt: she was Malera’s widow. Alone. Why had Putta brought him here? Putta himself was silent now, the man who was always chattering had fallen quiet. He felt as if two eyes were watching him from behind his back. It seemed to him that he had become an object, a thing, for those watching eyes. He was afraid to turn and look. And yet, there was desire. What would those eyes say? The moment eyes meet, what formless thing might take shape? Long, dark eyes. The braid of hair, black as a serpent, resting on her chest. On her...
Samskara

The swinging girl, bangles—wings, the clatter and flutter, in the forest, in the darkness, her full breasts thrust forward. Naked breasts, the color of silvered earth. Eyes behind her back, unblinking, that see everything laid bare like an object on display. A bird, helpless and afraid before the eyes of a black serpent. They turned away. Yes. Eyes that, holding the plate in hand, glanced furtively... Eyes peering from the doorway slipped away into the darkness. A bangle clinked. She returned to the light. Calm. A longing etched itself into the body, a restless expectation circling within. As she bent to set down the plate, her sari slipped, her breast thrust forward. A gaze heavy with desire. Fire coursed through his chest. His eyes leapt and devoured her. The feeling of being an object laid bare before the eyes behind her back vanished like a mirage. Now he himself was those eyes. Tat tvam asi.
"Where are you from?" Padmavathi asked, looking at the acharya, who seemed radiant.
"Kundapura," said Putta.
"I know Sheenappaiah," he lied.
"He manages the temple affairs," another lie.

"He has come to this region for collection work," he gave himself yet another new identity. In the eyes of strangers, a new form, a new disguise. In a single day, he had become so many different people that even he doubted who he truly was. So be it. Let what has happened, happen. They sat waiting. The bird that had been caught, the bird that had surrendered. Bangles. As if a fresh, living soul had been touched. Bhagirathi, shrieking like a kite, collapsed, spent. Once again, his tapasya-bhoomi blazed with fire. He had lost it. He was corrupted. Fallen before these eyes, he had sacrificed himself to a ghostly state, perhaps atonement.

Padmavathi, careful not to meet his gaze directly, went and sat at the foot of the door. Sitting thus, knowing she was watching him, Praneshacharya once again grew restless. He summoned his courage and turned his neck. His heart pounded. Padmavathi stood up.
Samskara 129

She brought in the betel leaf tray and set it down. She smeared lime on a small leaf, pressed the areca nut into the crease of her fingers, tossed it into her mouth, and began to speak. Padmavati sat again at the threshold, near the door. Putta said:

“We met the Acharya on the road. We kept talking as we walked. They were heading out by the Kundapura road. I told them—‘Stay here tonight, and tomorrow you can go to Tirthahalli and catch the bus.’ Isn’t that right?”
Padmavati, shy but insistent, said:
“Of course. You must stay here tonight and leave in the morning.”

To Praneshacharya, it felt as if he were about to faint. His ears rang, his hand trembled. No. No. Not today. I did not imagine that the moment I was to decide tomorrow could arrive so suddenly, right now. Not today. I am in mourning. I have just cremated my wife. Narayanappa’s corpse is still not removed. It is rotting. Vultures have come and perched on the house. I must speak out. I must tell the truth. I must get up and run away from here. Disappear. But his body sat there, solid and unmoving, an object of Padmavati’s expectant gaze.
Putta said:
“All right then. They haven’t eaten yet. They’ll eat at the temple. The Dharmasthala fair is here, isn’t it? Will you go to see it?”
“No, Putta. I’ll go in the evening, have darshan of the deity, and return. I’ll wait for you.”

Without a word, between Putta and Padmavati, the decision of his life was made. “Come,” said Putta. The Acharya stood up. He looked at Padmavati. Her hair, oiled and washed after her bath. Thighs, hips, breasts full with flesh, tall and shapely form. A glow in her eyes. Expectation waiting. She must have bathed with five sacred waters, like Pushpavati. Her chest rose and fell with her breath.

If pressed, they emerge in the darkness. The scent of fragrant grass. Flickering, flickering fireflies, fire—climbing the firewood, then climbing hands and feet, roasting in the belly with a sizzle, tearing, bursting, the flame that slices through the marrow and licks the chest with its tongue. Narayanappa’s corpse, still unburnt. How Mahabala, muttering, sat himself upon the chavadi. It swung and swayed upon the bamboo pole. Yajnavalkya called out and spoke: Love. Love for whom? Love called wife, love for myself, love called God, love for myself. I seek the root. I shall win. They watched, they approved, in the boat Vyasa was born holding the kamandala. He walked on. “Then go, if you must. I will wait,” said Padmavati. Most of all, Maruti withdrew his hand. Mahabala deceived. Narayanappa settled his score. The Brahmins coveted gold. Chandri stood in the darkness—she gave—she walked away. Bhagirathi, torn, died. Putta placed his hand on my back. He stopped at the edge of the field. “What do you say?” he asked. “It happened just as I imagined,” I replied. “Don’t think they are low people, Marayare. There wasn’t a single Shudra lurking nearby. She isn’t one to yield even to ordinary Brahmins. Not for money, not for coins. Didn’t you see? There is a garden. Even sages must lose their hearts—so it happened to her. I was anxious, thinking you might expose my lie somewhere. But you agreed, didn’t you? This Putta will do anything for friendship. ‘The Benefactor Putta’—that is my title,” he said, laughing, patting my back. Crossing the field, over the fence, across the stream, walking through the lane, back into the bustle of the fair. People around the chariot. People around the soda shop. People around the monkey-dancer. Children’s whistles, balloons. Amidst all this, a ghost, a demoness. Beating the drum, someone stood in the crowd and shouted: “There is plague in Shivamogga—”
Samskara 131

A loudspeaker blared: “Those traveling to Shivamogga must get inoculated at Tirthahalli; this is a municipal warning.” The people listened with curiosity, then resumed sipping their soda. They burst into laughter at the antics of the dancing monkey. A bilingual man, fluent in both Urdu and Kannada, was selling medicine to the gathered crowd: “Just one anna, ek anna, ek anna. For stomach ache, ear pain, urinary troubles, rheumatism, children’s cough, skin diseases, scabies, typhoid—this pill is the cure. Prepared by learned Malayali pandits, only one anna. Ek anna, ek anna….”

A man with a Bombay trunk danced. “Look, Tirupati Thimmappa! Look, Bombay prostitute!” On the sloping ground beneath a thick rope tied from a tree branch to the earth, a Dom boy slid down, came to a halt, and saluted. A mother slapped her son who had begged for a balloon; the boy cried. From the coffee hotel, the gramophone played a song. At the shop in the alley, sweets of every color were on display. The voices of the Gowdas and Heggadatis rang out in their characteristic tones. On the chariot, mantras were chanted in a rapid murmur. The Smarta Brahmins conversed in their brisk, clipped speech.

Now, here, in this very moment, a decision must be made. Should he abandon the twenty-five years of his samskara and become a man of this world? No. First, Narayanappa’s funeral rites must be performed. Only then can he decide. Today, Garuda Lakshmanaru would arrive, having received the Guru’s command. If the Guru refused, what should he say? The same old dilemma.

He stood near the temple. A blind man, clutching a harmonium, sang a dasa’s song: “How shall I praise and worship you?” Seeing a coin placed in the blind man’s bowl, another beggar, crippled in both arms and legs, crawled over, waving his stunted hand and crying out, “No arms, no legs! No arms, no legs!” He lay down, lifted his legs and arms, slapped them, displaying the places where his fingers had rotted away and become festering wounds.
Praneshacharya, in his mind…
Samskara
