The sight of the decaying body, the corpse of Naranappa festering without the rites of samskara, returned to his mind. Putta drew another small line in the dust. More bodies writhed, crawled, clutched their bellies, slapped their mouths, and pushed their way in. "Go, go," said the Acharya.
"You go and eat, then come back," said Putta.

"You come too," said Praneshacharya. Suddenly, he felt anxious at the thought of being seen by the Brahmins sitting for their meal in the temple courtyard without anyone by his side. He felt he could not move without Putta. Never before had he felt that he could not bear to be alone like this.
"You speak well. Have you forgotten that I am a Malera?" said Putta in response.
"Don't worry, come," said Praneshacharya.

"Are you making fun of me? Most of the people in this gathering know me well. Otherwise, I would have tried my luck. Hey, don't think I've never done this before. I've eaten at the choultry in Udupi. Who asks questions there? Hey, you know that a Sonnegara's boy lied and got a job in the matha. If you look at it that way, do we not have a sacred thread? I only said it for the sake of conversation. I am not so eager to eat with you. You go ahead. I'll wait here."
Unable to bear the droning chant of the waiting bhikshukas, Praneshacharya, confused, walked inside.

Banana leaves had been spread on all four verandas of the temple. Before each leaf sat a Brahmin, ready for the meal. As Praneshacharya looked at their faces, his heart thudded with fear. What if he was found out? He felt like running away. But he could not lift his foot. He stood rooted, lost in thought.
Samskara 137

He shuddered: What am I doing? What kind of Chandala act am I committing? I am in a state of impurity, and yet, knowingly, should I eat with these Brahmins? Should I defile them all? These are people who believe that if even a shadow of impurity touches the chariot, it will not move forward. If I sit here and eat, it is as if, by seizing Ganapati’s honor, I have destroyed Brahminhood just as Narayanappa did—a corrupt act. And if, while eating, someone discovers that I am Praneshacharya… if they realize I am impure… there will be an uproar. The entire chariot festival will come to a halt. A thousand eyes will devour me.
“There’s a leaf here. Come, come.” He was startled. He looked. A Brahmin sitting at the end of the row was calling him. What could he do? O Lord, what could he do? He stood still.

“Didn’t you hear me call?” The Brahmin who had called him smiled and took his hand, showing him the empty leaf. “Look, I placed a tumbler on the leaf for you. Otherwise, you would have had to wait for the next round,” he said. Mechanically, the Acharya went and sat with him. His head began to spin.

Trying to steady his mind, he thought: Lord, where is the root of this fear? Is this the torment from a previous birth? Is it the anxiety of being discovered? How can I uproot this fear? Is this the same fear that would end if I slept with Padmavathi tonight? The same fear that would vanish if I went away and lived with Chandri? What is the price of my resolve? Am I doomed to this ghostly state, unable to make any decision at all?
I should have stayed back. Should I get up and leave? What will the Brahmin next to me think?

A Brahmin walked along the row, letting his authority brush the edge of each leaf. Behind him, another poured payasa at the edge of each leaf with a spoon. Behind him, two sturdy Brahmins carried rice…
Samskara

...serving, they called out, “Dāri, dāri, dāri.” Again, kosambari, cucumber palya. With each new dish brought, a new face appeared, and with it, a flicker of unease—what if I am acquainted with this one? The one sitting beside me, the one who handed me the leaf—a Brahmin, dark as Bhīmasena, with a broad, powerful frame. A Smārta, who had drawn sandalwood paste across his nose. Just the sight of him had unsettled the Acharya. And then his questions, each one more disconcerting:

“Where are you from?” “Down the ghats.” “I am from this town. Where down the ghats?” “Kundapura...” “What community?” “Vaishnava.” “Which sect?” “Shivalli.” “We are from Kota. Your gotra?” “Bharadvaja.” “We are of the Angirasa gotra. Mahārāya, it is a great pleasure to make your acquaintance. I have a daughter, Swami. In another year or two, she will come of age. We are not yet so fallen as to marry her off before she is ready. So I am searching for a suitable groom for her. If you know of any eligible young man from your side, please let me know, Mahārāya. It would be a great favor, like lifting the burden of a kanya. After the meal, do come to my house. I will give you a copy of her horoscope. It would be good fortune if you could stay with us tonight.”
Praneshacharya, as he had sambar poured onto his rice, looked up. The one serving the sambar was watching his face—paused for a moment—then moved on.
“Let it be,” said Praneshacharya, wishing to end the conversation there.

Could the one who came to serve this sambar possibly know me? There was a streak of ash on his forehead. He was a Madhva—enough for him to recognize me. If I were to get up now, the parimanchane would be disturbed; I was already holding the tirtha in my hand. I had already sipped it, chanting “Shrimad Ramaramana Govinda Govinda.” The hot rice was mixed with sambar and eaten. How many days had it been since I last ate a proper meal? O Paramatma, deliver me from this calamity. Just for today, let me remain unnoticed. I cannot resolve that this is my decision alone, for once I decide, others become entangled in it as well. After all this, I should have performed Narayanappa’s samskara. But how could I do it alone? Three more would be needed to lift the corpse. I would have to ask them. If I did, their Brahminhood would be implicated in my decision. This is the root of my anxiety and distress. Yet, as it happened when I joined with Chandri, I drew the entire agrahara’s life into my action. As a result, my own life became an object laid bare before the world’s eyes.
The one who served the sambar returned, calling out again, “Sambar, sambar!” He stood before his leaf plate and said, “Sambar.” Fearfully, Acharya raised his eyes.
“I have seen you somewhere,” the man said.

“Perhaps,” replied Acharya. The man, by the grace of God, went on serving sambar to the next row. His eyes lingered on me; within his mind, he was searching for my image, trying to recall where he had seen me. Even if I went away with Chandri, someone would confront me and ask, “Who are you? What is your gotra? What is your lineage?” Unless I completely renounce my Brahminhood, I cannot be free of this. But if I renounce it, I will fall, like an insect into the tiger-marked world of the outcastes, to be burned and destroyed. How can I escape this haunted state?
“For the second helping of sambar, they have mixed water into it,” someone remarked.
The Brahmin sitting beside him said, “Why do you fill your stomach with just the sambar? The main dishes—rice and sweets—are yet to come. Wait.”
The one who had brought the sambar now served the sour curry, moving down the same row, standing before him.

“I can’t quite remember where. Maybe it was at the matha? Sometimes I go there to help with the cooking for the worship. Our agrahara is across the river. Just the other day, I cooked for the worship at the matha and came here,” he said, ladling out the curry, repeating “huLi, huLi, huLi,” as he served another row.
He thought of getting up and leaving now. But his legs felt as if they were made of wood. The Brahmin beside him continued,
“Our girl is clever in the kitchen. She’s obedient to her elders. Our wish is to marry her into a big, respectable kulina family where her parents-in-law live with her.”

There was only one way to escape this fear: he must take responsibility for Narayanappa’s funeral rites. He must stand before the Brahmins of the agrahara, among whom he had grown up with such dignity, and declare it. He must call Garuda and Lakshman and say: This is what has happened. This is my decision. I am casting aside, before your very eyes, the noble character I have cultivated in your midst. I have come to throw it away in front of you. Otherwise, this fear will never leave me, and I shall never be free.

Then—just as Narayanappa had overturned the life of the agrahara by dishonoring Ganapati, so too would he destroy the Brahmins’ way of life. It would be a thunderbolt to their faith. What could he say? He had consorted with Chandri. He had looked upon his wife with shame. He had drunk coffee in a hotel. He had wagered on cockfights.

I went. I was drawn to Padmavati. In the end, even when I was in *sootaka*, I sat and ate with the Brahmins in the temple. I even called a boy from the Malera caste to eat with us. This is my truth. It is not an admission of guilt. It is not the remorse of a sinner. It is simply a harsh truth. The truth of my inner life, and so it is my resolve. Through this resolve, look, I have severed myself.

“If you wish, there is no objection to giving dowry, Mahashayas. Because these days, times are so bad that it has become difficult to marry off dark-skinned girls. If you come and see the girl, you will see—except for her dark skin, she has all the features: eyes, nose, all the marks. According to her horoscope, she has Gajakesari Yoga. She will bring Lakshmi into the house she enters.”
The Brahmin sitting beside me said this as he ate *huli anna*.

But, unless I told the Brahmins of the agrahara, unless I performed the *samskara* for Narayanappa’s corpse, the fear would not leave me. If I decided, without telling anyone, to live with Chandri, it would not be complete. Now, I must make a complete decision. Everything hidden must become manifest. It must be set before the eyes. Yet, there is anguish either way: if I keep it hidden, there is the anxiety that someday it will be exposed to someone’s eyes; if I reveal the truth before the Brahmin eyes that shaped me, there is the fear that their lives too may be thrown into confusion by it. There is the anxiety—do I have the right to draw another life into the circle of my resolve? Cowardice. O God, relieve me of the responsibility of making a decision. Let this resolve happen as if in the darkness of the forest, in the night, it happens by itself. Let a new birth come before I close my eyes. Narayanappa, did you too have this anguish? Mahabala, did you suffer it as well? I must ask.
The one who served the *saaru* came again, filling the basket with *laddus* and serving them. The Brahmin beside me, without placing the laddu on his leaf, with his left hand—
He took the plate and set it aside. Then he stood before his own leaf. His chest thudded.

"No, what should I say to my wife if I am ruined? Aren’t you Praneshacharya of Durvasapura? Should someone like you come here and sit for a meal? There was a grand feast at the moneylender’s house, with chiroti and all. All the elders were satisfied there. I didn’t realize at all because there was no vibhuti or akshate on your forehead. And you didn’t say anything either. If I don’t tell the moneylender, I’ll be punished for it—serving a meal to a great pandit in a lowly place. Wait here, I’ll be back in a moment,”

he said, putting the ladle back in the pot and running off. Praneshacharya, resigned, rose quietly and walked away. “Swami, Swami, there’s still payasa to come!” called the Brahmin beside him. Without turning back, he walked out of the temple. He hurried away, unwashed hands, keeping far from people, farther and farther. As he walked, he heard: “Acharya... Acharya...” It was Putta’s voice, small and eager. Putta ran up and stood beside him. Praneshacharya quickened his pace.
“What’s this, Marayare? Not a word, not a story, just running off—as if you’re in a great hurry for something important,” Putta laughed.
Once they were far from people, Praneshacharya stopped. He looked at his sticky hands and felt ashamed.
“What, even in washing your hands you’re in a hurry, Marayare? That’s happened to me too. Come, let’s go to the tank.”
They started walking towards the tank. On the way, Putta said:

“I’ve made up my mind, Acharya—I’ll come with you to Kundapura tomorrow morning. I didn’t tell you. My wife and children went to their maternal home a month ago. No letter. I must use my wits and bring them back. You are an elder, a Brahmin.”

Is it not so? Do me a favor—speak some sense into my wife. She will listen to your words. In a single day, you have become my dearest friend. And another thing, Acharya, I am not one for gossip or slander; by my mother’s oath, I will not tell anyone that you slept in Padmavati’s house. I was only standing there watching the monkey’s dance, Marayare, and when I saw you running, I could not help but laugh. Isn’t it true that when one is eating, sometimes there is a sudden hurry? Perhaps that is all it was, and so I laughed.”

Praneshacharya descended into the tank and washed his hands. On the bund above, Putta stood with his back leaning against the parapet. After washing his hands, Praneshacharya came and stood beside him.
“So soon? What is it?” Putta asked.
“There is something, Putta.”

Praneshacharya looked up: the long summer evening. In the west, a red glow was spreading. Lines of white egrets were making their way home. Below, at the edge of the tank, a heron croaked. Soon it would be time to light the lamps. How many days had it been since the lamps were lit in the agrahara? How many days since the cows, returning from the byre at dusk, were tied up and called, since the offering was made to the gods? The outlines of the Western Ghats on the horizon were fading, as if the world itself were melting into a dream. The colors of this moment would vanish in another instant, leaving the sky bare. The new moon must have passed—soon, the rim of the moon would appear above the foreheads of the hills, like the edge of a silver plate bent in ritual anointment. In the valleys between the hills, silence would settle deep and thick. As the night’s worship ended, the lamps would burn dim, and the tumult of the festival would subside. Again, the sound of the drummers from the fair would rise and spread. If I leave now, I will reach the agrahara by midnight—far away from this world. In the frightened eyes of the Brahmins, a fresh, trembling life...

Standing apart, I become a stranger among them in the ancient midnight that lies between us. Perhaps, as the flames circle his corpse, there is a certain peace. When I speak, there must be no taint of regret, no sorrow that I have become a sinner. Or perhaps the conflict will never leave me. I must see Mahabala. Is it true, at least, that only the form we attain in our resolve can be claimed as truly ours, and that is what I must tell him? If so, should I not ask you—do you now have no longing for God at all?

“Lalita lavanga lata pari sheelana komala malaya samare…” The verse fluttered in Praneshacharya’s heart, filling him with a deep yearning. Love had come upon him. For the first time, he placed his hand on Putta’s shoulder, drawing him close, patting his arm as he said, “I was about to say something…”

“No, Marayare,” Putta replied, delighted that the Acharya had placed his hand on his shoulder. “When I met you on the road, seeing the gravity in your words, I thought—these are not the kind of people who would befriend someone like me.”
“Look, Putta, do you know why I left my meal in such haste? I must leave for Durvasapura this very moment.”

“Oh, how is that possible, Marayare? Your Padmavati will be waiting there, having prepared a fresh meal, lit incense, and arranged flowers. How can she face you if you are not by her side? No matter how urgent or necessary, you must stay here tonight and leave only in the morning. If you leave now, I will not allow it,” Putta said, gently restraining Praneshacharya.
A sudden fear gripped Praneshacharya. He wondered if he might melt away from his own resolve. He had to escape from this Putta.

“No, Putta, it is absolutely impossible. Shall I tell you the truth? I did not tell you because I did not want to trouble your mind.” He paused for a moment, wondering what to say, and decided that it would be safer to utter a lie: “My brother…”
Samskara 141
It was only when I sat down to eat that I learned he was lying sick with a terrible fever in Dhoorvasapura. Now, when he might pass away at any moment—how could I...”
He let out a small, hopeless sigh.
“Well then,” said Praneshacharya, preparing to leave, “Should I see you again? If you take the road to Kundapura, tell Padmavati I will come to see her. Should I set out now?”
Putta stood there, thinking. “How can I let you go alone, in this darkness, through the forest path? I’ll come with you.”
Now Praneshacharya was at a loss. By no means could he send this man away. “You’ll only be troubled by me, there’s no need,” he said. But Putta would not relent.

“It’s no trouble at all. No hardship, no suffering. I have some business in Dhoorvasapura too. I have relatives in Parijatapura. You know Narayanappa, that’s enough for an introduction. When you visited Parijatapura, you met them just as you met him. Ah, Marayare, I’m glad you reminded me. The whole town knows how Narayanappa’s property was squandered. Among the women who gossip with their saris pulled over their heads, she is one. Let it be, Marayare. If you know her, please don’t mention that Padmavati called you. Why keep secrets from you? It was only after meeting Narayanappa that I got entangled: he asked me to introduce him to Padmavati. I’m not the sort to meddle in such things, you see. But once a Brahmin gets entangled, what can be done? Yet Padmavati did not approve of him; she called him a drunkard and said, ‘Don’t bring him here again.’ Let it all remain with you, Marayare. I don’t know why I started talking about all this...”
Samskara

It was abandoned. I told you, didn’t I, that our village lies beyond Tirthahalli? There, the Narayanappa family owns a garden. It has fallen into ruin, leveled with the ground. For years, not even a single areca nut from it has come into their hands. Isn’t it familiar? They say they don’t know me, but I thought I’d try asking. ‘Lease the garden to me. I’ll revive it, and make sure you get your share of the areca nuts,’ I said. To that, he replied, ‘In the darkness, even a path finds its people. It’s good for both of us.’

Praneshacharya, still restless, listened to Putta’s words. Should he tell him that Narayanappa was dead? Should he reveal his true predicament? But he could not bring himself to trouble such a simple heart with such a great confusion. If, by chance, Putta did not accompany him, it would be impossible to keep it secret—so he thought. Suddenly, Praneshacharya felt that if Putta were with him, he would have company. How could he face all those Brahmins alone? First, he would confide in Putta, who had become so close. To see what would appear in his eyes—that too was a good plan.

Now the sky was completely bare. From the temple came the sound of conches and drums. He had to hurry. If he stood here any longer, someone would find him, and the donor would come searching. ‘If you’re going, let’s go,’ he said.

Just then, a bullock cart came down the road towards them. ‘Wait a moment,’ said Putta, stopping the Acharya. He raised his hand and halted the cart. From inside, a Brahmin wrapped in a jerisalle poked his head out and asked, ‘What is it?’
‘Is your cart going by way of Agumbe?’ Putta asked.
‘Yes,’ replied the man inside, wrapped in his shawl.
‘Is there room for two? We’re headed towards Durvasapura,’ said Putta.
Samskara 143
“There is space for only one person, isn’t there?”
Little Praneshacharya took his hand and said, “You go, Acharya.”
“No, let’s both walk together,” said the Acharya.
“Don’t, don’t tire yourself walking so far. Come and see tomorrow, please,” said Little.
The one wrapped in a shawl hurried them: “Well then? Are you coming or not? We’ll turn back a mile or two past Durvasapura. If one of you wants to come, come quickly. Come soon.”
Little pushed Praneshacharya insistently. Praneshacharya, helpless, climbed into the cart and sat inside.
The cart set off. “I’ll see you tomorrow,” said Little.
“So be it,” said Praneshacharya.
It was done. Now, four or five hours of journey ahead. And then?

Now, stars in the sky. The crescent moon. The Saptarshi constellation standing bold. Suddenly, the sound of drums. Here and there, the glow of bonfires. The breath of the oxen climbing the hill. The bells at their necks.
Four or five hours of journey. And then?
Praneshacharya waited, in expectation, in anxiety.

Dup!

A crow landed on the roof. Praneshacharya, who had been sitting in meditation, opened his eyes. The early morning light filtered through the plantain leaves, casting trembling shadows on the courtyard. The agrahara was still, save for the distant cawing of crows and the faint tinkling of a temple bell.

He rose slowly, feeling the stiffness in his knees, and glanced at the sacred tulasi plant in the courtyard. The rituals of the day awaited him, but his mind lingered on the sound—dup!—the crow’s arrival, a mundane event, yet laden with meaning. In the agrahara, even the smallest sign could be an omen, a message from the gods, or a reminder of the cycle of life and death.

Praneshacharya walked to the threshold, his thoughts already turning to the unresolved question that troubled the hearts of all in the agrahara: what rites should be performed for Naranappa, the rebel who had scorned their customs and died an untimely death? The crow’s call seemed to echo the uncertainty that hung over them all.
